records.title: Nutritional Problems in Patients Who Have Chronic Disease
records.abstract: After completing this article, readers should be able to:Nutritional problems in chronic disease are a significant cause of increased morbidity, mortality, and psychosocial consequences of growth failure. Several mechanisms may coexist that could lead to nutritional problems. Mere increased inflammatory burden can increase the caloric need and, thereby, the risk of protein-calorie malnutrition. The organs involved, such as the liver and small bowel, may be important in the digestive and absorptive processes, and their Winvolvement may lead to selective nutrient deficiencies. Anorexia of chronic disease may coexist and compound the situation. Although this discussion focuses on general principles in specific areas, attention to detail in individual cases is needed.Nutrition support can be achieved at several levels. Dietary counseling leading to better choices in caloric density can be augmented by using specific high-calorie commercial preparations to boost caloric intake. Occasionally, a multidisciplinary approach with a feeding team can help with issues relating to gastroesophageal reflux and delayed gastric emptying as well as oral skills and behavioral aversion, which can optimize intake. Nasogastric tube feeding and, for long-term use,gastrostomy tube feedings are the next step. These devices allow delivery of appropriately chosen milk-based formulas either in convenient bolus regimens or continuously, as needed. Continuous nocturnal feeding regimens are particularly popular because they allow oral intake when awake, yet increase the caloric intake. These generally are safe techniques that can be taught easily to caregivers.Nasogastric tube feeding can lead to problems with reflux, chronic irritation in the oropharynx and distal esophagus, sinusitis, and nasal septum deviations after long-term use. If long-term use is predicted or becomes apparent after 3 months of feeding, use of the gastrostomy tube is a better alternative. This method also is generally well tolerated and reversible. If gastric feeding is not well tolerated, jejunostomy may be required.Cystic fibrosis (CF) impairs growth and weight gain (including fat and protein maldigestion through fecal loss), increases susceptibility to infection, and decreases longevity.Patients who have CF experience major increases in energy requirements because of intestinal losses and recurrent respiratory tract infections. The need for additional energy leads to increased energy expenditure, which in turn accentuates the need for additional energy intake. Depending on the severity of respiratory insufficiency, estimates have placed caloric requirements for children who have CF at 120% to 150%of the recommended daily allowances (RDA). Unfortunately, the patient’s needs often are not met and are complicated by vomiting induced by coughing, anorexia that accompanies chronic pulmonary insufficiency, and increased effort to breathe. Other factors that may impede energy intake include reflux esophagitis and chronic malaise.Nutritional support is an integral part of the management of patients who have CF. Much of the improvement in longevity documented over the past decade may be attributed to the focus on improved nutrition. Therapy also should encompass psychosocial issues because compliance can be a major hurdle, and a large number of measures may be needed to keep nutrition optimal. Supplementation with pancreatic enzymes is used to enhance intestinal absorption. Supplements should be administered if there is even a slight chance of pancreatic insufficiency;intervention will prevent large energy and protein losses through fecal loss. Enzyme supplements can increase fat absorption up to 80% to 90% of all ingested fat, but attempts to improve on this percentage by increasing enzyme supplements,such as by using high-potency preparations, can lead to colonic strictures. Fat-soluble vitamins are encouraged, as are aggressive and invasive means of dietary support,such as nighttime nasogastric or gastrostomy tube feedings.In 35% to 65% of children who have chronic renal failure (CRF),linear growth is decreased, and more than 50% of children who have end-stage renal disease suffer growth retardation. Reasons for altered growth are multifactorial and include metabolic, hormonal, and nutritional abnormalities. Because undernutrition is prevalent, children who have CRF present with many of the signs and symptoms of protein-energy malnutrition,including stunted growth, decreased muscle mass, decreased skinfold thickness, increased serum growth hormone, decreased somatomedin-c,and low weight for height. Anorexia due to “uremic toxins” is one of the causes of reduced food intake. Others include altered ability to taste and drug therapies specific to CRF.It is particularly important to maintain growth in the first 2 years of life because moderate-to-severe malnutrition at this age is associated with cognitive problems, even if subsequent catch-up growth can be achieved. Specialized formulas,assisted feeding devices, and close follow-up may be needed. Linear growth and weight gain often can be maintained with adequate caloric intake.The goal of nutritional therapy for children who are in end-stage renal failure depends, to a large extent, on the degree of renal insufficiency. No one “renal failure” diet can be applied to every case. Nutritional management, together with such other therapeutic modalities as hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis(intermittent and continuous),transplantation, and prolonged conservative management must be individualized. Nutritional intervention is paramount. Most published studies agree that among children receiving less than 70% to 80% of RDA for height, additional energy intake will improve growth and restore tissue mass. Growth hormone therapy has been shown to increase linear growth in infants and children who have chronic renal insufficiency, and apart from possible long-term concerns with hyperinsulinemia, has been shown to be well-tolerated. The response is blunted if renal osteodystrophy is significant, and this condition can increase the risk of avascular necrosis or slipped capital femoral epiphysis.Fifty percent of children who have cancer suffer from malnutrition. Although not present in all pediatric malignancies, protein-energy malnutrition is a serious and common occurrence in many cancers,including stages III and IV Wilms tumor,stages III and IV neuroblastoma,pelvic rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, multiple relapse leukemia,and medulloblastomas.The development of malnutrition depends on certain characteristics of the malignancies, such as anatomic location, type, and tumor-specific therapy. A malignancy of the oropharynx can interfere with feeding due to neck or head surgery or mechanical obstruction. Patients who have leukemia can have accelerated basal metabolic rates. Additionally,many patients undergoing chemotherapy for advanced stages of malignancy suffer from nausea,vomiting (with associated fluid and electrolyte loss), and diarrhea.Anorexia also is common, and its causes are both psychological and biologic. The development of aversions to certain foods because of taste disturbances while receiving gastrointestinal-toxic therapy adds to weight loss. Stress among young patients frequently can play a role in malnutrition and decreased food intake. Nutrient malabsorption due to surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or graft-versus-host disease includes incomplete ingestion of fat protein and carbohydrates. In addition, carbohydrate metabolism generally is abnormal in cancer, leading to impaired use of energy and protein. Finally, children typically have additional metabolic demands for normal growth. Although the etiologic role of nutritional factors in any type of malignancy is not clear,a good nutritional state allows for more aggressive and effective treatment, which may reduce the rate of relapse. Enteral feeding should be considered initially, but parenteral nutrition may be needed during times of prolonged anorexia.Factors to be considered in such aggressive nutritional support include: current nutritional assessment; identification of potential nutritional problems; appropriate therapy; monitoring of therapy; and effective communication with patients, parents, and primary physicians.Nutrition requirements in the neurologically challenged child can vary substantially, depending on various aspects of the neurologic deficits. For example, bulbar or pseudobulbar palsy and oral aspiration often necessitate the use of assisted feeding devices, with gastrostomy tubes increasingly favored for long-term use.Caloric needs can vary from as little as 50% of expected requirements in children who have little or no movement to greater than 200%of expected requirements in those who have athetoid cerebral palsy.Protein intake often needs to be higher than normal in proportion to caloric intake. Goals of ideal weight for length are to maintain growth at the 5th to 10th percentile if the patient is not ambulatory after the first 2 years of age. It is important to note that additional calories will lead to weight gain, but not to an increase in lean body mass. This can affect mobility adversely.Constipation and gastroesophageal reflux with delayed gastric emptying often require specific nutritional changes, such as fiber-containing formulas and low-volume continuous feedings with iso-osmolar or hypo-osmolar milk-based formulas. Regular assessment of weight can assist in titrating the caloric needs. Indirect calorimetry may be used to help predict caloric needs.Growth problems are common in congenital heart disease, often relating to the severity of the malformation. Cyanotic lesions tend to impair both height and weight; acyanotic lesions with left-to-right shunts impair weight more than height. Although prenatal factors, such as associated syndromes, may impair growth, postnatal factors are more common. These include a hypermetabolic state from increased cardiac effort, reduced splanchnic blood flow, tissue hypoxia, and frequent infections. Certain situations,particularly after a Fontan procedure, lead to increased gut protein loss and malabsorption. Despite increased caloric needs of up to 175 kcal/kg or more, voluntary caloric intake does not appear to increase to meet the demand, probably because of fatigue due to coexisting increased respiratory and cardiac work and early satiety from delayed gastric emptying in congestive heart failure. Anorexia also may be a complication of drug therapy with digoxin and potassium. High-calorie nutritional supplements and, if needed,nasogastric tube feeding can be effective with careful attention to fluid balance. Surgical correction often results in dramatic catch-up growth with the same amount of calories.Vitamin deficiency is the most prevalent outcome of protein-energy malnutrition. Depletion of water-soluble vitamins occurs more frequently than that of fat-soluble vitamins. Vitamin B12 works in conjunction with iron and folic acid to produce red blood cells. Inadequate intake of both vitamin B12 and folic acid inevitably leads to anemia. In addition, a deficiency in folate can result from inadequate intake,absorption, transport, or utilization.Deficiencies in both B12 and folic acid often result from congenital errors of metabolism and rarely are associated with deficits. An undiagnosed vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to irreversible neurologic damage.The B complex vitamins include thiamin (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin(B3), nicotinic acid, nicotinamide,pyridoxine (B6), folate, vitamin B12,cynocolbalamine, pantothenic acid,and biotin. Maintenance of positive vitamin B status is predicated on adequate consumption of all members of this complex. Therefore,utilization of one vitamin often is affected by the consumption of another. Furthermore, because a single food rarely contains only one vitamin, a diet deficient in one vitamin may be deficient in others,especially in cases of protein-energy deficiency. Single vitamin deficiencies are usually rare and limited to such specific diseases as juvenile megaloblastic anemia (folate) or disease of the terminal ileum(vitamin B12), when the consumption of a specific drug inhibits absorption or metabolism of a particular vitamin.Patients who have chronic diarrhea or congenital malabsorption as well as drug interactions should be monitored closely for folate deficiency. Folate deficiency also may result from an increased requirement, such as that observed in hemolytic anemias.Folate deficiency can be diagnosed by observing hypersegmented neutrophils and macrocytes in a peripheral blood smear. A serum folate level less than 6.81 nmol/L(3 ng/mL) and red blood cell folate level less than 317.8 nmol/L(140 ng/mL) indicate deficiency. Megaloblastic change and asynchronous nuclear-cytoplasmic maturation in the bone marrow is a further indication.Most forms of folate deficiency are not evident in early infancy due to large supplies of vitamin B12. Exceptions include inherited disorders of B12 metabolism and megaloblastic anemia in the breastfed infant of a B12-deficient mother. Diagnosis is based on a serum vitamin B12level of less than 100 pg/mL(<75 pmol/L) and hypersegmented neutrophils in the early stages. Progressive deficiency may be associated with megaloblastic anemia,megaloblastic changes in the bone marrow, leukopenia,thrombocytopenia, and mild jaundice. Neurologic manifestations may precede anemia. Posterior and lateral column demyelinization in the spinal cord and associated paresthesias may be evident. Other symptoms include sensory deficits, loss of deep tendon reflexes, slowing of mental processes, confusion, and memory defects.Treatment for folic acid deficiency includes a therapeutic dose of folate of 0.5 to 0.1 mg/d. This may be administered safely during repletion after the diagnosis has been established. Inappropriate administration of large doses of folate can aggravate neurologic manifestations.Treatment for vitamin B12deficiency involves an intramuscular dose of 50 to 100 mg. Vitamin B12deficiencies not attributed to poor diet require chronic monthly injections.Multiple food allergies can lead to major problems in maintaining an adequate nutritional balance. The diagnosis is difficult to accept unless inflammation is confirmed on mucosal biopsies and symptoms are elicited repeatedly in blinded food challenges. Synthetic formulas based on the use of amino acids or hydrolyzed cow milk protein are available for all ages and can supply all the nutritional needs, although they are expensive. Specific problems include low calcium and fat intake in milk-avoidance diets, low vitamin B12and iron in diets that also avoid meats, and an increased likelihood of suboptimal intake of other micronutrients. Prospective 3-day dietary assessment and evaluation should be performed in these situations.

records.title: Online Attention Competition and Polarization Among Beijing’s 5A–Level Tourist Attractions: A Baidu Index—BCG Matrix Analysis for Sustainable Destination Management
records.abstract: In the digital era, online attention has become a key indicator of tourism competitiveness and destination visibility. This study proposes a two-dimensional framework to evaluate the competitive state of online attention by combining its current magnitude and growth dynamics. Using Baidu Index data, the study applies the Boston Consulting Group (BCG) matrix and the coefficient of variation to analyze online attention patterns of Beijing’s 5A–level tourist attractions from 2011 to 2025. The results show clear polarization in online attention. A small number of iconic attractions consistently dominate digital visibility, while many other sites exhibit unstable and uneven attention trajectories. These patterns reflect the cumulative effects of consumer behavior, information-seeking preferences, and algorithmically mediated content environments, which reinforce attention concentration and competitive inequality over time. External shocks, particularly the COVID–19 pandemic, caused sharp declines in online attention in 2020, followed by an uneven recovery in subsequent years, highlighting the volatility of digital attention systems. The study also demonstrates the managerial value of the proposed framework. By classifying attractions according to attention levels and growth potential, the framework supports differentiated marketing and demand–redistribution strategies. For instance, increasing the visibility of high-potential but under-visited attractions can help redirect visitors away from overcrowded “Star/GC” sites and encourage more balanced spatial and temporal visitation. Overall, this study proposes a quantitative and replicable framework that integrates digital attention dynamics, algorithmic filtering, and consumer behavior into destination competitiveness analysis. The framework supports evidence-based and sustainability-oriented destination management by informing adaptive marketing and demand management strategies that can help alleviate overtourism and balance visitor flows. However, the study relies on a single digital platform and lacks direct sustainability indicators. Future research should integrate multi-platform data and link online attention metrics to measurable environmental, social, and economic sustainability outcomes.

records.title: Outfoxed: Design and Evaluation of a Modular Interactive Puzzle for Cognitive Enrichment of Zoo Animals
records.venue: International Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
records.abstract: Cognitively stimulating experiences are fundamental to supporting the welfare of zoo-housed animals. Puzzle-feeders are often initially engaging, but require frequent human intervention and often lack adaptability to support animals’ sustained cognitive engagement. We developed a modular adaptive puzzle-feeder designed to support user agency, independence, and multisensory feedback. The system was deployed over four weeks with an Arctic fox (Vulpes lagopus) across progressive difficulty levels and piloted with two coatis (Nasua narica). Combining HCI and animal science methodologies, we assessed (1) multisensory engagement, (2) changes in behavioral diversity and habitat utilization, (3) adaptation to puzzle complexity, and (4) impact on human stakeholders. Results show strong sustained engagement (46.5% time-budget), increased behavioral diversity, habitat exploration, strategic problem-solving, and positive keeper and visitor reactions. This work highlights how technology can support animal welfare and visitor experience, and how mixed HCI and ethological methods enable holistic evaluation of enrichment and animal usership.

records.title: Paying Less Generalization Tax: A Cross-Domain Generalization Study of RL Training for LLM Agents
records.abstract: Generalist LLM agents are often post-trained on a narrow set of environments but deployed across far broader, unseen domains. In this work, we investigate the challenge of agentic post-training when the eventual test domains are unknown. Specifically, we analyze which properties of reinforcement learning (RL) environments and modeling choices have the greatest influence on out-of-domain performance. First, we identify two environment axes that strongly correlate with cross-domain generalization: (i) state information richness, i.e., the amount of information for the agent to process from the state, and (ii) planning complexity, estimated via goal reachability and trajectory length under a base policy. Notably, domain realism and text-level similarity are not the primary factors; for instance, the simple grid-world domain Sokoban leads to even stronger generalization in SciWorld than the more realistic ALFWorld. Motivated by these findings, we further show that increasing state information richness alone can already effectively improve cross-domain robustness. We propose a randomization technique, which is low-overhead and broadly applicable: add small amounts of distractive goal-irrelevant features to the state to make it richer without altering the task. Beyond environment-side properties, we also examine several modeling choices: (a) SFT warmup or mid-training helps prevent catastrophic forgetting during RL but undermines generalization to domains that are not included in the mid-training datamix; and (b) turning on step-by-step thinking during RL, while not always improving in-domain performance, plays a crucial role in preserving generalization.

Predicting Flow State and Learning Engagement in
 GAI
 ‐Powered Virtual Influencer‐Mediated Informal Foreign Language Learning
records.abstract:
This study examines the role of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI)‐powered virtual influencers in enhancing foreign language learning engagement within informal digital environments in China. Drawing on the Hedonic‐Motivation System Adoption Model, we develop and test a theoretical framework that incorporates perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, joy, perceived behavioural control, parasocial relationships and flow state. Using structural equation modelling to analyse survey data from 368 Chinese college English learners engaged with GAI‐powered virtual influencers on Bilibili, our findings demonstrate that perceived behavioural control emerges as the most significant predictor of both flow state (
 β
  = 0.342,
 p
  < 0.01) and learning engagement (
 β
  = 0.524,
 p
  < 0.001), as well as the importance of perceived ease of use. The study reveals that parasocial relationships (
 β
  = 0.177,
 p
  < 0.01) and joy (
 β

 p

These results advance our understanding of technology‐mediated foreign language learning by highlighting the unique mechanisms through which GAI‐driven virtual influencers facilitate learning in informal settings. The research provides practical implications for designing educational technologies that effectively combine entertainment and pedagogical value to optimise learner engagement.

records.title: Research on Mobile E-Commerce App Experience Design Based on Flow Theory
records.abstract: This study is grounded in flow theory and aims to investigate how applying flow-based design principles can enhance user engagement and satisfaction in mobile e-commerce apps. First, the paper reviews the core elements of flow theory and summarizes the current state of experience design research for mobile e-commerce apps, identifying common challenges and shortcomings in existing design practices. Next, it constructs an experience design model based on flow theory. By combining literature analysis with expert interviews, the study identifies key design dimensions — such as "challenge–skill balance", "immediate feedback", and "intrinsic motivation" — as the most influential factors for enhancing flow in mobile e-commerce experiences". In the design practice phase, a representative mobile e-commerce app is selected for prototype redesign. Usability testing and quantitative surveys are used to evaluate and analyze user experience. Research findings indicate that introducing appropriately challenging task guidance in interface interactions, strengthening real-time feedback mechanisms, and creating a guided achievement system can significantly enhance users' sense of immersion and willingness to continue using the app. Finally, based on user testing and empirical data, the paper summarizes several feasible flow-driven design strategies and offers suggestions for future research improvements and practical applications, providing theoretical and methodological support for mobile e-commerce platforms to build differentiated user experiences in an increasingly competitive environment.

records.title: Social media marketing in the business interaction system of the enterprise
records.venue: Herald of Kyiv National University of Trade and Economics
records.abstract: Introduction. The digital economy is deve­loping very quickly in the world, so all busi­nesses understand the need to use modern interactive technologies in predicting consumer behavior and are ready to adapt the informa­tional potential of campaigns to the conditions of global digitalization. Problem. The digital economy accelerates changes in marketing communications and requi­res new relevant channels of digital interaction. The aim of the article is to substantiate the selection and implementation of modern digital marketing communications in the business envi­ronment of the campaign in order to predict con­sumer behavior and develop entrepreneurial infor­mation potential. Methods. Methods of systematization, grou­ping and comparison, analytical and epistemo­logical methods (for assessing the state and prospects of the use of social networks), graphic and analytical methods (for illustrating research results), abstract-logical analysis (for resear­ching the evolution of marketing communica­tions), and Internet monitoring (to determine the effectiveness of the most relevant channels of digital marketing communications, their ranking by popularity) were applied in the paper. Results. The authors determined that social networks during the war became the fastest, most effective and most accessible channels of communication with the audience. Social media marketing channels and their rating were analyzed; the most relevant for the enterprise – B2C and B2B consumers – were justified in the context of the development of the information potential. Conclusions. The necessity of increasing the monetization of digital marketing communica­tions and strengthening their communicative effectiveness in the context of a two-way app­roach is proven. On the one hand, it is necessary to improve the quality of content and its delivery methods to consumers, commercial activities that ensure the finalization of acts of purchase and sale and delivery of goods and receipt of services. On the other hand, monitor the existing and potential channels of digital marketing com­munications, respond to their popularity among different types of consumers, scale the use of digital technologies, facilitate the accessibility of their use, improve the information infrastruc­ture, strengthen the digital trust and technolo­gical competence of specialists, as well as form a new digital business culture.

records.title: Who Will Provide Care for People With Complex Physical Disabilities?
records.abstract: This issue of PM&R includes an “Invited Perspectives” article that profiles Dr Henry Betts. My conversation with him has led me to reflect on his question of whether it has been a good idea for our field to expand to champion musculoskeletal and sports rehabilitation [1]. As chairman of the Department of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation at The Rehabilitation Institute of Chicago (RIC) at the time, he had resisted the change, concerned that it would distract physical medicine and rehabilitation (PM&R) from its core mission—that is, the care of people with permanent disabilities. As evidence that his concern might have been prescient, Dr Margaret Turk, in her 2008 Walter J. Zeiter lecture, noted that musculoskeletal medicine, pain management, and electrodiagnosis are now the fastest growing segments of our profession [2]. The related question of who should be providing primary care services for people with disabilities was vetted in the 1990s. In the wake of managed care and the “gate keeper” concept, Dr Bruce Gans and colleagues not only from PM&R but also from pediatrics, family practice, and internal medicine raised the following questions: Who is the most appropriate primary care physician for people with disabilities? [3] Should PM&R physicians aspire to this role? What role should other primary care specialties play in the care of people with disabilities? We now need to revisit these questions, especially in the context of health care reform, because the medical home concept for the care of patients, particularly those with complex conditions, is being re-energized [4, 5]. The question of whether PM&R physicians should assume the role of providing a medical home is becoming increasingly urgent for patients with childhood-onset disabilities who are aging out of the pediatric care system, where care coordination has been much more the norm than in the adult care system, as evidenced by specialty clinics that provide coordinated care for children with spina bifida and neuromuscular diseases [6, 7]. In short, our health care system is ill prepared to provide the type of preventive health, holistic, and primary care services needed by people with disabilities. People with disabilities have complex conditions that require coordination of care, and yet our health care system has become increasingly fragmented and poorly coordinated [8]. The number of people with disabilities is growing, and their needs will only become more pressing. They experience unequal access to health care services and significant health care disparities. We are not preparing as a profession to meet these needs. Health care professionals in general are not routinely trained to provide care for people with disabilities, and PM&R residency training programs are still the place where the most specialized training takes place [9]. It is a precarious situation and raises fundamental questions for our field about our professional responsibilities to advocate for potential solutions. These questions were posed to the following commentators: Bruce M. Gans, MD Kessler Institute for Rehabilitation Margaret Stineman, MD University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine Stuart Willick, MD, FACSM University of Utah Orthopaedic Center Elie Elovic, MD University of Utah M.Elizabeth Sandel, MD Kaiser Foundation Rehabilitation Center Current President, AAPM&R As always, we invite you to share your thoughts and opinions in Letters to the Editor. It is not unusual to hear strongly held opinions and heated debate among a group of physiatrists (especially a multigenerational group) when the question is raised of the role of PM&R in treating patients with disabling conditions versus those with musculoskeletal impairments. Dr Kirschner has posed a number of highly relevant questions that poke at the issues of care for people with disabling conditions, the social responsibility of our field, the difference between personal interests and a profession's responsibilities, and what we are obligated to do about it all. There is no doubt that our field was born with one foot in the comprehensive rehabilitation camp and the other in the physical medicine camp. Our roots seem to have condemned us to perpetuate this debate. Originally, the discussion was about treating patients with war injuries versus looking for ways to apply physical agents to human illnesses. Today, the debate could be formulated as treating patients with serious disabling conditions versus those with musculoskeletal impairments. It also could be described as the dichotomy between physicians who want to take care of inpatients (with its accompanying lifestyle) and physicians who want to work with outpatients. Some overlap of this dichotomy may be seen, but these are certainly the typical terms for a debate (or a job search, for that matter). Who should take care of people with disabling conditions? Historically, very few people in any specialty have wanted to do it. PM&R physicians came along in very small numbers and raised their hands to say, “We'll do that!” Most other physicians either were relieved that someone else was willing to step up to the challenge or believed that we were foolish to waste our time on the “hopeless who could not be cured.” As a matter of fact, when I was a medical student, I vividly recall being told by one of my neurology attending physicians that “you're too good to waste your time in rehab.” One man's meat is another man's poison, I guess. Yes, physicians in some other specialties have risen to meet the needs of certain patients with disabling conditions, and we all know who they are: pediatricians for some children with developmental or early acquired conditions, rheumatologists for patients with serious joint disease, cardiologists for some cardiac patients, geriatricians for the frail elderly, neurologists for some patients with neurologic conditions such as multiple sclerosis or stroke, and orthopedists for some patients with disabling musculoskeletal conditions. However, the care of persons with disabling conditions in each of these specialties is really a minor component of the overall specialty, practiced by a small number of individuals who, I guess, “aren't too good to waste their time at it.” Thus PM&R is really the only specialty that was “chartered” to serve this clinical and social need. I personally believe it is a triumph whenever we can attract a physician from another specialty to adopt the values of our field and choose to care for “our” patients. I know that some physiatrists are threatened by the encroachment of these alien specialists onto our turf, but, honestly, as long as they are eager to help, will do it right, and know what they do not know, I say, welcome to the party! Should PM&R assume primary care responsibility for persons with disabling conditions? Back in the 1990s, important incentives to be declared a primary care specialty seemed to be emerging. Our efforts to popularize the role a physiatrist could have in the primary care of certain patient populations was motivated by a desire to try to serve their needs and to get PM&R recognized for this effort. Our model in Detroit really was what would now be described as a medical home—a multidisciplinary team (ie, a physiatrist, internist, nurse practitioner, therapists, and case managers) organized to deliver primary care around protocols and standards of practice. It required the infrastructure of an organization (the Rehabilitation Institute of Michigan) to make it work, but work it did [1]. I believe all of those program attributes would be relevant and appropriate to replicate in today's world of medical homes and accountable care organizations, but I am not at all sure that the economic incentives to do so will strike a resonant chord with the existing potential providers (PM&R groups, multidisciplinary groups, and inpatient rehabilitation hospital-based practices). I hope they do, but only time will tell. What is the role of training programs (and also the Residency Review Committee and the American Board of PM&R)? Should they yield to the veritable flood of young physicians entering our training programs who seem to show not just strong preferences for musculoskeletal medicine but possible active aversion to inpatient rehabilitation? The short answer is “no.” I believe it is perfectly fine—in fact, of value—to have this strong flow of well-qualified physicians entering our world. In general, they have bolstered our ranks, strengthened our numbers, and added many positive dimensions to our specialty. But I believe our training programs have an obligation to preserve the essence of medical rehabilitation and to acculturate all our practitioners to embrace its values and support it, even if it is not their personal choice for practice. It is better to keep the core values of PM&R intact and treasured than to allow them to be lost in the mists of time. Thus striking a balance in the training and testing between rehabilitation and physical medicine (just like always) is still the right thing for our Board, Residency Review Committee, and programs to do. If we continue to preserve the common values (ie, function and role in society) along with the technology (eg, ventilator management of a patient who is tetraplegic and insertion of a needle under ultrasound guidance), then all should be well with the world—if: If the field as a whole continues to fight for the medical care needs of people with disabling conditions in the halls of Congress, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, and the insurance companies. If the field continues to innovate to provide that care in better and more economically efficient but clinically appropriate ways. If the field advocates for research funding and conducts the needed research with those funds to make it better. If the field partners with others (eg, other specialties, hospitals, and consumer groups) to promote the notions of social justice and access to care and services for all persons with disabling conditions who need it. If our training program leaders embrace responsible ways to work with other specialties to train people well, in collaboration, and to encourage those who want to “waste” their career by taking care of persons with disabling conditions, regardless of their specialty of origin. As an organized specialty and as individual physicians, society grants us many privileges, but it expects responsible conduct that is in the best interest of all persons, not just the self-interest of our own practitioners, in return. If we put into practice the ideas I have expressed here, we will earn the right to continue to be treated as a respected profession. I woke slowly to a musty plastic odor. The pain grabbed me with my first conscious breath. The love in my mother's eyes, seen dimly through the yellowed wall of the plastic oxygen tent, calmed my heart. Above the tight bandages about my chest, the skin felt puffy, too soft and no longer like my own. I was 6 years old. My parents met a surgeon at a party where I was running about with other children. He said he could “fix my deformed chest” and make me “look more normal.” At the time he proposed this procedure, open heart surgery was not yet commonplace. He told my mother that he had held my beating heart in his hands to move it under my sternum in preparation for cutting away the deformed costal cartilages on the left side of my sternum. After the procedure, my pigeon breast deformity was indeed diminished, but although I looked more normal, I never ran again. I did not have the breath. I sank when I tried to swim. As a child, I wished the surgeons would stop trying to fix me with procedure after procedure but instead use their medical knowledge to empower my function for full participation in life. Later in my life, PM&R and vocational rehabilitation colleagues did empower me and continue to do so. records.title: Write more, worry less: A guide to enhancing your academic productivity
records.abstract: Writing a manuscript can be intimidating, but it's an essential skill that can be honed with practice. In “How to Write Better,” I discussed some technical aspects of writing.1 This follow-up article focuses on starting your writing journey, establishing an effective writing routine, and mastering the iterative writing process. I present actionable strategies and illustrate these principles with clear examples from my experiences. Whether you're a novice or a seasoned writer, I hope this guidance inspires you to write more. One of the most common misconceptions about writing is that great writers are born with innate talent. In reality, great writers are made through consistent practice. Writing helps you develop your voice and refine your style. Writing regularly keeps your mind engaged in the writing process. The more you write, the better you write. Any form of writing counts, and you can practice your writing while being productive. I learned to write by writing editorials, case reports, short clinical reviews, and Op-Eds for local news organizations.2 Writing these types of shorter articles will help you build the skills and discipline necessary to tackle larger projects with less worry.3, 4 It can be hard to just sit down and write. However, don't fall into the trap of waiting till the mood strikes you. If you're not in the mood, you need to set it. Develop a routine that primes you to write and identify the conditions under which you write best. Leverage this structure for your writing sessions. For instance, if listening to music while sipping tea gets you in the mood to write, start each writing session with those activities. If you prefer writing in short bursts amid a busy day of meetings, schedule 30-min writing blocks. If a quiet, distraction-free environment is more conducive to your productivity, consider libraries, co-working spaces, or writing at home whenever (if ever) it's quiet. If a bit of background noise helps you focus, find a coffee shop with the right level of hustle and bustle. Over time, you may find that you experience a Pavlovian desire to write when you start your routine under your preferred conditions. I generally write best when I block out larger chunks of time (i.e., 3–5 h); the noise level and the surrounding activity matter less to me. I typically spend more than half of that time thinking about what I'm going to write. I start by sitting in front of my computer with a blank page open on the screen, a notebook in front of me, and a pen in hand. I'll run through ideas in my head and occasionally scribble some words on paper. If I'm stuck, I may write, “What am I trying to say?” on the paper before me as a prompt to organize my thoughts. I'll begin typing when I have a general sense of what I want to convey. Once I have written a few paragraphs, I carry a printed version with me and use brief moments of downtime (e.g., my dentist's waiting room, soccer halftime) to do a little self-critique, as described below. Finding time to write in the context of our other responsibilities can be challenging. Clinical schedules, teaching sessions, committee service, and other activities compete for time. For these activities, there are also others, whether division directors, colleagues, or trainees, to hold us accountable, while in writing, we're usually only accountable to ourselves. No wonder it's easy to let writing fall by the wayside. Blocking out dedicated writing time in your schedule can help keep you on track to write regularly. The act of scheduling writing on your calendar creates commitment, which makes it easier to follow through. For self-accountability, it's important to treat this time as nonnegotiable, just like any other important commitment. Dedicated writing time allows you to create a routine and signals to your brain that it's time to write. Consistency is key, whether it's every morning, a few evenings a week, or even a few hours every few weeks. As with exercise, when I'm writing regularly, I crave it and make time to write. Manuscript writing is inherently a solitary task, but that doesn't mean you have to do it alone. Sharing your progress, discussing challenges, and celebrating milestones with others can make writing more enjoyable and less isolating. Working alongside other writers can also introduce you to new ideas, perspectives, and approaches. This community of fellow writers can enhance your progress by providing motivation, support, and accountability. Writing partners and peer mentorship groups can meet in person or virtually.5 These partnerships require participants to coordinate their schedules, which naturally leads to blocked writing time. Larger academic programs have also leveraged writing retreats to advance scholarship while building community.6 Single-day retreats can easily be integrated into the work week, while multiday retreats require some planning and a small financial investment. As you develop your writing group, keep in mind that longer writing blocks (e.g., 90 min) may work better early in the day when energy is higher, and shorter writing blocks (e.g., 45–60 min) may work better in the afternoon as focus wanes.6 The blank page can be daunting, but the most important step in writing is simply to start. Get some words on paper. They don't have to be good; they just have to be words. They may not feel perfect or even good, and that's okay. When you focus on putting words on paper instead of worrying about whether they're any good, you capture fresh and unfiltered ideas. This process can help clarify your thoughts and lead to new insights. The goal of a first draft isn't to produce a masterpiece but rather to create a scaffolding upon which to build. If you're sitting there staring at a blank page, reflect on what I occasionally say to my mentees, “I can't edit what you haven't written.” I begin writing by creating a document listing the major manuscript headings: Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. I start with this step because it helps me overcome the inertia of getting started. When I return to the manuscript later, I've already started writing, allowing me to focus on continuing to write rather than attempting to start. I usually tackle the methods section next. The structured subheadings (e.g., study design, setting, participants, interventions) are useful writing prompts. I can complete this section and circulate it to the team for review before the study is finished. For me, the rest of the manuscript comes together in a less regimented manner. I focus on writing different sections or creating tables and figures depending on my mood. Embrace the iterative nature of the writing process. View each draft as an opportunity to refine your work and move closer to a polished and cohesive final piece. What I might refer to as a first draft is usually the result of me repeatedly rewriting each paragraph after self-critique. However, if you find yourself stuck, it can be helpful to bounce some ideas off a colleague. I never number my manuscript drafts as “version 1” or “version 2”; instead, I label each version by date, starting with the year (e.g., Write More 2024-07-15), so my different manuscript versions sort sequentially. I save these different versions so that I can revisit deleted phrases, paragraphs, or ideas if necessary. If I make substantive changes on the same day, I add sequential letters to the date (e.g., Write More 2024-07-15a). I share this quirk to emphasize the dynamic process of writing where there is no definitive first or second or, dare I say, final version, but rather a living document that continuously evolves. Learning how to critique your own writing is an essential skill. You shouldn't do this while you're writing; otherwise, you'll hamper progress. However, you shouldn't wait until you have a complete draft to review it with a critical eye. The key is to find a balance between writing and self-critique. For example, you might review and edit your work near the end of a writing session or whenever you're stuck and unsure what to write next. This may feel awkward at first but, over time, it becomes second nature. To critique my writing, I print out what I've written and read it from a reader's perspective. This shift in mindset is beneficial because now I'm too focused on trying to understand what I've written to worry about writing. With a pen in hand, I'll ask myself whether each paragraph logically flows from the preceding one. I'll often write the theme of each paragraph in three to four words in the left margin to help me in this process. I then concentrate on individual paragraphs, mapping the ideas in each sentence to determine whether they connect in a meaningful sequence. This step helps me understand whether the paragraph makes sense and identifies redundancy. We all get attached to sentences or phrases we love. Sometimes we must let them go to serve our larger goal of writing well (Figure 1). Feedback is an invaluable part of the writing process. You are better off receiving the toughest feedback before the manuscript has been submitted; it makes the peer reviewer comments seem easy to address in comparison. Of course, your co-authors and mentors will review your manuscript. Also, seek out others who can provide constructive criticism. Colleagues who are not involved in the work can offer perspectives and insights you might not have considered. Do not take any comments personally. Those who provide constructive feedback care enough about you—and your work—to devote their time to helping you improve it. And don't be flustered by divergent comments. Different reviewers may have different opinions, so you should weigh their suggestions and decide what works best for the manuscript. One of the biggest obstacles to productive writing is the pursuit of perfection. However, the notion of perfection is at odds with good writing. The writing process is messy, and striving for perfection causes frustration and procrastination, hindering progress. Additionally, the path from manuscript start to finish is not linear, making progress sometimes difficult to assess. Our colleagues and mentors can help us step back and take a broader perspective to evaluate progress. We must also be prepared to accept that our final version won't be perfect. Scientific writing isn't poetry; its purpose is to communicate a message clearly, and there are many ways to do that effectively. For those with a background in literature, this perspective might help you let go of the need for artistic phrasing, elaborate vocabulary, or striving for that ever-elusive “perfection.“ The key is recognizing when it's worthy of being submitted. To paraphrase French writer and philosopher Voltaire, perfect is the enemy of done. In summary, writing can be difficult. Don't worry about producing a polished manuscript. The goal is progress, so write more, worry less, and embrace the iterative process. The authors declare no conflict of interest.

records.title: ‘In‐betweeners’ in turbulent times: Migrants in the epicentre of diverse ‘crises’ in the Americas and Europe
records.abstract: This Special Issue (SI) brings together a selection of articles connected by the interplay of two main concepts or ideas. The first one refers to the fact that we are living through increasingly unstable and challenging times, defined by a succession of ‘turbulences’ that are often characterized as overlapping and interconnected ‘crises’ – a so-called era of ‘polycrisis’ with implications in multiple domains (Henig & Knight, 2023). In this global context, diverse phenomena interpreted as crises can bring about or impede migration, trigger the implementation of certain policies, and have an impact on migrant experiences and strategies. Existing work has focused on the links between migration and global crises, for instance, in response to the impact of the 2008 Great Recession (see Tilly, 2011, for an international perspective; Lafleur & Stanek, 2017, for the European context; Sassone & Yépez del Castillo, 2014, regarding migration between Latin America and Europe). However, the situation has evolved since as other turbulences occurred, including the 2015 ‘refugee crisis,’ the COVID-19 pandemic, and the Venezuelan humanitarian and migration ‘crisis.’ Aware that turbulences are not a new phenomenon at the international level but a key concept in assessing major transformations (Rosenau, 1990), our SI highlights the speed and broad repercussions of recent changes in which people on the move appear in a central position. The second concept relates to the figurative notion of migrants as ‘in-betweeners’ – i.e. occupying intermediate or diffuse positions not just in space and time (Crawley & Jones, 2021; Gius, 2021) but also in terms of migration categories, political practices, mobility strategies, and family relations. The articles in this SI explore how migrants as in-betweeners often find themselves at the epicentre of turbulent scenarios, portrayed alternatively as threats, victims, scapegoats, or agents. In this respect, our main goal is to investigate the (re)definition of migrants' positions and roles in such scenarios and how their strategies intersect with policy frameworks. To do so, we focus on the intersections between policy and agency at local, national, regional, and transnational realms, thus bringing in a diversity of relevant units and levels of analysis in the understanding of the global context (Panizzon & van Riemsdijk, 2019). Moreover, the articles encompass case studies from two world regions that are rarely analysed together in the migration literature: Europe and the Americas − including North and South America (exceptions include Aysa-Lastra & Cachón, 2015; Margheritis, 2018; Sassone & Yépez del Castillo, 2014). Although this SI per se is not comparative, we attempt to generate a cross-regional dialogue and invite comparisons between the two regions, and further afield. Our SI is indeed the result of a muti-year interdisciplinary collaboration guided by such goal.i The following sections explain in depth the theoretical and conceptual rationale of the SI, setting it in connection to the existent literature and highlighting the main contributions of the individual articles. The articles here investigate the diverse ways in which lived experiences, public discourses, social practices, and policies define the image and roles of people on the move during diverse crises. Scholars in the Global North and South have addressed the emergence of migration and crises from various angles. Whitin the former, for instance, some studies highlight the impact of crises on the framing of policy alternatives that are proposed as responses, providing a helpful baseline for conceptualization (McAdam, 2013; Scholten & Van Nispen, 2015). Others alert us about the disjuncture between analytical and policy categories and the lived experiences of people on the move (Crawley & Skleparis, 2018). Analyses of international migration in the context of crises also tend to build on case studies and state-level variables (Lindley, 2014) or focus on global governance approaches (Martín Díaz & Aris Escarcena, 2019). These works, largely revolving around immigration and refugee concerns, do not always account for the new open-ended mobilities connecting unstable contexts or the growing precarization of migrant statuses and lives, especially in connection to migration between (and within) Europe and the Americas (exceptions include Aysa-Lastra & Cachón, 2015; Bermudez & Oso, 2020; Lafleur & Stanek, 2017; Padilla et al., 2016). Regarding perspectives from the Global South, Latin American scholarship on migration and crises has addressed this largely at the national level in response to several economic, political, or social crises (e.g. Jokish & Pribilsky, 2002; Pellegrino, 2002). Some of the latest studies reflect that the entire region currently struggles with long-standing and recent interconnected challenges, including refugee flows, mass emigration, intra-regional mobilities and return migration (Bengochea & Pellegrino, 2023; Herrera & Gómez Martínez, 2022). Yet, most empirical studies revolve around the national and local levels of analysis. Works on the challenges posed by the recent massive displacement of Venezuelans in the region are a case in point (e.g. Gandini et al., 2020). Except for a few works (e.g. Geddes et al., 2019; Margheritis, 2018; McIlwaine, 2011; Sassone & Yépez del Castillo, 2014), studies integrating cross-regional analyses between the Americas and Europe are very scarce. The articles in the SI seek to go beyond some of these limitations. They all assume that migration today is generally taking place in the context of high instability or unsettling turbulences, leading to fluid (im)mobilities and representing a major challenge regionally and globally. This might affect especially those mobilities that are more prone to vulnerability, such as ‘irregular migration’ or refugee flows, which are the focus of several articles in the SI, but also flows that are regarded as more privileged, as the texts by Bermudez and Roca, and Escrivá, Bermúdez Figueroa and Minguela show in the case of intra-European Union (EU) mobilities. We also problematize the taken-for-granted notion of crisis by focusing, at the empirical level, on diverse turbulences shaping migration flows, policies, and migrant experiences in the two continents. These include the so-called Great Recession, the political-economic-humanitarian crisis in Venezuela, the volatile migration and refugee contexts in Europe and the USA, as well as other social impacts of neoliberalism and the COVID-19 pandemic. Our articles seek to go beyond the idea of crisis as a sudden, external shock that alters a “stable and functioning system” to acknowledge “the diverse forces and agencies that produce what comes to be understood as crisis over long spans of time” (Dowler, 2020). Moreover, we argue that global instability and increasing uncertainty are very much context-dependent, with geography − or space, at various scales (Glick Schiller & Çağlar, 2011) − playing a key role. Accordingly, bringing together insights from two world regions is a starting point in the quest for plausible and empirically grounded explanations. In this respect, the article by Margheritis on migration governance evolution in South America serves as a conceptual anchor for the rest of the SI. She uses the concept of ‘nested crisis’ to underline that the Venezuelan ‘migration crisis’ in South America is better understood as “embedded in a larger context characterised by diverse, interrelated critical conditions/junctures.” The proposed concept highlights the relevance of not only analysing the policy choices and constraints that mark migration governance transformation in crisis-prone contexts, but also fostering cross-regional discussions. From a European perspective, the text by Bermudez and Roca applies the notion of ‘intersecting crises’ to elaborate on how events ranging from the Great Recession to the recent pandemic have impacted the (im)mobility strategies of intra-EU Spanish migrants, generating both new vulnerabilities and opportunities. The articles by Aris Escarcena, Filippi, and Anderlini contextualize different types of irregular migration in Southern Europe within wider displacement trends caused by recent conflicts. They show that these developments have triggered constant policy reformulations and contestation about the ways in which migration should be managed. Other contributions to the SI frame specific events and experiences at the local level within wider processes. These discuss, for instance, the housing crisis affecting Peruvian migrants in Buenos Aires as part of historic gentrification pressures (Cuberos-Gallardo); mutual aid responses to COVID-19 from migrant groups in New York as potential stepping stones towards structural transformations (Délano Alonso and Daria Samway), and the production of ‘fitful circulations’ in Sicily as the result of experiments in border control that are the consequence of the interaction between (g)local markets and migrant agency (Anderlini). In addition, the text by Herrera, Carrillo Espinosa and Lara Reyes on Ecuadorian migrants in Europe during the pandemic, provides a broader approach to understanding the different meanings of crises for transnational migrants. The notion of migrants as ‘in-betweeners’ in turbulent times works here also as a central image that all the contributions in the SI evoke, albeit in different ways. Overall, this notion highlights that migration has an intrinsic element of transition between a place of origin and one or more destinations and between moments in time in a migration trajectory, as movement situates people in intermediate positions or in-between spaces and points in time. For authors like as Crawley and Jones (2021), the idea of in-betweeners helps understand better migrants' material and symbolic journeys, rather than focusing on linear narratives between ‘origin’ and ‘final destination.’ For others, like Gius (2021), being in-between may refer to different time-based migration flows within the same community (e.g., Italian migrants in Toronto). However, our SI goes beyond these meanings to consider more broadly the many ways in which migrants are sometimes positioned or feel as in-between, especially in turbulent contexts. Growing and increasingly diverse flows, the politicization and securitization of migration, and the rise of nationalist ideologies, among other global trends, are recasting the figure of the migrant amidst diverse crises increasingly in dichotomist terms either as victims or villains (e.g., Herrera & Sørensen, 2017; Hintjens, 2019; Padilla & Goldberg, 2017). We argue that by being in-between ‘here’ and ‘there’ in turbulent contexts, migrants occupy not simply a physical but also a symbolic intermediate position, thereby becoming a pivotal (and often instrumental) element within multiple crises. While their role has been traditionally defined in reference to formal arrangements or legal frameworks, as in national citizenship regimes and international refugee norms, our SI zooms instead on the fluid and malleable category of in-betweeners to expose context-specific redefinitions of migrants' position and roles. Analysing migrant experiences and migration policies as embedded in critical junctures and protracted crises allows us to better capture the nuances, complexity, and tensions in the interplay of migrant agency and institutional processes. The articles in the SI thus revisit and explore empirically agent-structure dynamics by focusing on the various ways in which migrants find themselves in-between at the epicentre of diverse crises. In relation to this, we critically examine how migration discourses are politically constructed and migrant statuses and roles are (re)negotiated in the public and private spheres, offering empirical evidence and novel insights into debates about the politicization and securitization of migration under conditions of high volatility. In this respect, the articles by Martín-Díaz and Castellani, and Délano Alonso and Samway examine case studies in Spain and the USA, respectively, showing how the political strategies of the ‘subaltern’ evolved during the pandemic and its aftermath. The former analyses how the pandemic led vulnerable migrant women in Spain, many of them from Latin America, to develop digital political responses based on ‘creative bricolage’ that represented new responses to longer-standing struggles for full legal, labour, and social rights. The latter places collective strategies from migrant grassroot groups in New York amid government responses to ‘temporary’ turbulences and long-term policy frameworks. Aris Escarcena's contribution on the so-called campization of migrants and refugees in Europe also argues that the pandemic exposed not only the limitations and controls imposed by camps, but also their potential as sites of resistance and new political projects. Also, Cuberos-Gallardo's situates Peruvian families' strategies against residential expulsion from Abasto (Buenos Aires) in an ambivalent position as insiders (part of the local community)/outsiders (not nationals). By focusing on Spanish migrant families in other EU countries and the childcare decisions of dual-career couples, Escriva, Bermúdez Figueroa and Minguela's piece reveals the fragility of European care and welfare regimes and illustrates the persistence of gender norms that place women in a more vulnerable situation. As such, our SI goes beyond macro policy analyses, problematizing the intersection of public and private domains. By doing so we also interrogate processes of labelling and defining people on the move as migrants, mobile citizens, refugees, diasporas, etc., as well as current discussions of so-called ‘mixed flows’ (see Ghosh, 2018, among others). Filippi's contribution, for example, argues that the city of Rome has become a transit crossroads for “lifelong in-betweeners” or orbiters, a term that illustrates different mobility and policy situations since the 2015 ‘migrant and refugee crisis’ and the situation of those without a definite migration or citizen status. A final contribution of the SI relates to the geographic and analytical scope of investigation. While trade, finance, cultural, and population flows have historically linked Europe and the Americas, human mobility across the Atlantic received less attention than the circulation of other factors. The type, direction, and magnitude of cross-regional flows have changed over the centuries, prompting new approaches to rapidly changing demographic and migration trends. Both regions have transitioned from emigration to immigration, and vice versa, and many countries currently experience incoming and outgoing flows that include a growing diversity of migrant profiles (Margheritis, 2018). Furthermore, in these two geographical spaces, migration flows have proven to be rapid changing phenomena that call for timely interventions in sync with responses to unexpected instability. Yet, these regions are rarely apprehended as interconnected; compartmentalized perspectives preclude cross-regional fertilization. Hence, our SI looks at both continents under a common framework to shed light not only on the empirics of migrants being at the epicentre of crises but also on the lenses we use to understand this. Our goal is to encourage a cross-regional dialogue based on both migrant-based and policy/institutionally driven issues. We aim to illustrate how top-down and bottom-up dynamics intersect and influence each other. However, a caveat is in order: we do neither attempt to cover both regions equally, nor address all relevant intra- and inter-regional issues in a comprehensive fashion. The unintended unbalanced distribution reflects the bias in existing literatures within migration studies, within which an overwhelming number of academic works focus on Europe. It is indeed in the European experience that the notion of migration crisis has been ingrained in most studies for decades, thus paving the way to arguments about the emergence of a ‘crisis mode of governance’ (Sahin-Mencutek et al., 2022). In contrast, in the Americas, the migration crisis is either rarely mentioned in the North American-dominant debate on immigration policy, or relatively new in the South American context (Margheritis & Pedroza, 2022). By including case studies from Europe and both North and South America, we also open up an opportunity to identify lessons across regions/sub-regions and avoid the traditional bias of focusing only on North-to-South learning. Thus, what we offer here is various entry points to the main themes of the SI that help elaborate the proposed concepts and arguments at different levels of analysis. We aim at broadening the analytical focus beyond the nation-state and a single region. Eight out of 10 articles apply levels of analysis above or below the nation-state and/or dynamics between them. Thus, some of the contributions offer a more macro or inter-regional perspective, like Margheritis' on South America's response to the Venezuelan migration crisis and policy lessons beyond. Others, focus on the European or Southern-European context to analyse the interconnections between specific crises and transformations in intra-EU mobilities (Bermudez & Roca; Escriva, Bermúdez Figueroa & Minguela), or changes in migration and asylum policy (Aris Escarcena). While the text by Herrera, Carrillo Espinosa and Lara-Reyes uses a transnational approach to understand care and emotional responses to the pandemic based on migrants' in-between (origin and destination) understandings of crises and their own positions. Except for Martín-Díaz and Castellani, which focuses on the national level (albeit from a broader, virtual social media perspective), the rest of the articles link the local level of analysis with broader national, regional and global processes, looking at migrants and their strategies vis-à-vis capitalist pressures (Cuberos-Gallardo) and policy transformations (or lack of them) in increasingly hostile environments both in Europe (Anderlini; Filippi) and the Americas (Délano Alonso & it is around the level of analysis that we have the of the articles.
