records.title: A Review of Emotion-Aware Adaptive Virtual Reality Games for Player Emotional Profiling and Intelligent Personalization
records.venue: Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Information and Communication Systems
records.abstract: The idea behind emotion-aware and adaptive virtual reality (VR) games is to provide better user experience through dynamic changes in game mechanics based on users’ emotions and behaviors. The current state of research on VR games includes such topics as dynamic difficulty adjustment, physiological sensing, facial electromyography, electroencephalography, and adaptation driven by engagement. This paper summarizes existing research articles focused on affective profiling of VR players and adaptation in VR games regarding methods used, modeling approaches applied, adaptive algorithms implemented, and obtained results. Although many positive outcomes are claimed in current research papers, there are some limitations due to small sample sizes, short session times, lack of real-time multimodal approach, and insufficient ecological validity.

records.title: A Roadmap-Aligned Decision-Support Methodology to Identify Scaling Mechanisms for Physical Internet-Compliant Logistics Innovations: The IKIGAI Approach
records.abstract: The decarbonisation of freight transport and logistics is a central objective of current global and European climate strategies. However, logistics systems remain highly fragmented, characterised by low interoperability, heterogeneous governance structures, and limited process standardisation. These structural constraints hinder the large-scale adoption of innovative logistics solutions and collaborative services. The Physical Internet (PI) paradigm proposes a systemic transformation towards interoperable, standardised, and hyperconnected logistics networks, but its operational implementation requires structured methodologies capable of guiding innovations from pilot experimentation to scalable and PI-compliant deployment. The EU-funded IKIGAI project (GA 101202912) aims to accelerate the transition towards zero-emission, collaborative, and scalable logistics systems by operationalising Physical Internet principles within real supply chain ecosystems. Building on the Zero Emissions Logistics and PI roadmaps, the project advances five complementary Logistics Innovations (LIs), addressing technological, governance, regulatory, and market-related barriers to large-scale adoption. The PI Norm as a reference standard for scalable logistics processes Within IKIGAI, the PI Norm is conceived as a process standardisation backbone designed to operationalise PI principles in logistics services. It consists of a set of standardised operational processes aimed at enhancing interoperability, collaboration, and logistics efficiency across heterogeneous actors. The PI Norm integrates three interdependent components: standardised logistics processes, interoperable digital and documentation flows, and governance and compliance mechanisms ensuring auditability and replicability. By translating commonly accepted operational rules into formalised and shareable processes, the PI Norm reduces fragmentation and enables coordinated logistics services across networks of independent stakeholders. Consequently, PI Norm compliance becomes a key condition for the systemic scale-up of LIs and for their alignment with the evolutionary trajectories defined by the PI (ALICE-ETP, 2020) and ZEL (ETP, 2019) roadmaps. Pilot Logistics Innovations as methodological benchmarks The proposed methodology is validated through five Logistics Innovations representing diverse service typologies and operational contexts: • LI1: Online and offline trustee matchmaking and volume pooling for electrification and increased intermodality; • LI2: eFTI-compliant Collaborative Service Platform for SMEs; • LI3: Smart and synchromodal hubs for hyperconnected urban logistics; • LI4: Intelligent, standard end-to-end chain of custody for carbon emission calculation; • LI5: Open volume pooled governance for reusable standard modular boxes. They serve as methodological benchmarks to test the robustness, transferability, and replicability of the proposed workflow. By applying the same analytical structure across heterogeneous innovations, the project systematically identifies recurring barriers to scale-up and extracts a set of universal scaling mechanisms. These mechanisms are subsequently formalised into a reusable library intended to support future LI in accelerating their transition towards PI Norm compliance and roadmap alignment. Conceptualisation of scaling mechanisms along Roadmap pathways Within IKIGAI, scaling mechanisms are defined as actionable enabling factors supporting the structured evolution of LI from their current maturity level to a desired PI-compliant state. This perspective explicitly links scale-up to the roadmap logic of progressive standardisation, interoperability, and collaborative governance. The methodology therefore shifts the analytical focus from purely technological readiness to a multidimensional understanding of scalability, encompassing governance structures, interoperability capabilities, regulatory alignment, market adoption, and sustainability performance. This approach reflects the socio-technical nature of logistics systems and the need for coordinated transformation across multiple stakeholders and operational layers. Methodological Framework Step 1: Definition of scaling dimensions and target scenario (TO-BE) The first step of the methodology defines scale-up through a multidimensional framework composed of six scaling dimensions: operational scope, technological maturity, regulatory/policy/governance aspects, economic and market adoption, societal and organisational alignment, and sustainability and circularity. Each dimension is structured into discrete maturity levels, enabling a consistent and comparable representation of innovation readiness. LIs define their desired TO-BE scenario as a coherent configuration of maturity levels aligned with PI Norm requirements and roadmap trajectories. To support this process, five archetypal prospect scenarios (Baseline, Accelerated, Disruptive, Collaborative, and Transformative) are used to position each innovation according to its strategic ambition and ecosystem dynamics. A classification logic based on maturity thresholds and conditional checks ensures methodological consistency while accommodating the heterogeneity of innovation contexts. Step 2: AS-IS Assessment through customised checklists Once the target scenario is defined, the methodology proceeds with a structured AS-IS assessment based on customised checklists tailored to each LI. This evaluation captures the current level of process standardisation, interoperability, governance formalisation, regulatory readiness, market uptake, and sustainability performance and allows the systematic mapping of existing practices against the maturity requirements of the selected TO-BE scenario, highlighting structural misalignments across scaling dimensions. This diagnostic is relevant in collaborative logistics environments, where innovations often exhibit high technological maturity but limited governance or interoperability readiness. Step 3: Gap computation and prioritisation The third step consists of quantifying the gap between AS-IS and TO-BE states. To avoid uniform treatment of heterogeneous constraints, the methodology applies a multi-criteria prioritisation based on the Analytic Hierarchy Process. This approach enables the weighting of gaps according to their relevance for scale-up within specific operational contexts. The outcome is a ranked set of critical gaps that identifies the main bottlenecks hindering the transition towards PI Norm compliance, such as insufficient interoperability, fragmented governance structures, regulatory barriers, or limited stakeholder adoption. Step 4: Identification of Scaling Mechanisms and generalisation. In the final step, prioritised gaps are translated into targeted scaling mechanisms selected from a structured and evolving library. These mechanisms include, among others, replication and standardisation packages (e.g. standard operating procedures and KPI frameworks), interoperability enablers (data-sharing protocols and semantic alignment tools), governance mechanisms (trustee roles, decision-right matrices, and reusable contractual frameworks), regulatory alignment actions, and adoption support measures (onboarding and training schemes). The application of the workflow across the five LIs enables comparative analysis and cross-case learning. This benchmarking process allows the identification of recurring patterns in scale-up barriers and the extraction of universal scaling mechanisms that are not limited to a single pilot context. As a result, the methodology evolves from a pilot-specific assessment tool into a transferable decision-support framework capable of guiding diverse LIs in their pathway towards scalability, standardisation, and compliance with the PI Norm. References ALICE-ETP, 2020. Roadmap to the Physical Internet, s.l.: s.n. ETP, A., 2019. Roadmap towards zero emissions logistics 2050, s.l.: s.n.

records.title: A Study on Accurate Recognition and Dynamic Facilitation of Flow Experience Based on Multimodal Learning Analytics from a Data-Intelligence Integration Perspective
records.venue: Proceedings of the 2nd International Conference on Digital Management and Information Technology
records.abstract: To address the challenge of quantifying and regulating the flow state in real-time within digital learning environments, this study constructs a closed-loop “accurate recognition-dynamic intervention” system based on data-intelligence integration. The system synchronously and unobtrusively collects multimodal data encompassing physiological (heart rate variability), behavioral (micro-expressions), and interactional (clickstream) dimensions. Utilizing an XGBoost model integrated with an adaptive attention fusion mechanism, it achieves 93.2% accuracy in recognizing flow states. The research identifies operational sequence entropy and high-frequency power of heart rate variability as key computational features for distinguishing flow. Innovatively, a deep reinforcement learning algorithm is introduced to construct an adaptive instructional engine that dynamically adjusts task challenge levels based on real-time flow probability. A four-week randomized controlled experiment demonstrates that this intelligent engine significantly enhances learners' flow experience frequency (Experimental Group: 4.32±1.21 times/week vs. Control Group: 3.12±1.45 times/week, p<0.001) and long-term knowledge retention rate (94.8% vs. 87.3%, p=0.011). This study provides a complete technical pathway and empirical evidence for advancing next-generation personalized education from “state perception” to “state shaping”.

records.title: A Systematic Review of AI-Driven Game Design and User Experience Research
records.abstract: In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly integrated into game design, driving innovation that extend from development efficiency to user experience. This study systematically reviewed the research on user experience in AI-driven game design published between 2020 to April 2025, analyzing 74 studies retrieved ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore and Web of Science. Findings indicate that AI has been incorporated into all stages of game design, enabling collaborative development and facilitating personalized content adaptation and real-time player interaction through dynamic difficulty adjustment, affective computing, and generative technologies. The integration of multimodal technologies further enhances immersion and engagement. In cross-domain applications, AI-driven serious games demonstrate strong potential in fileds such as education and healthcare. Nevertheless, challenges remain in terms of technology integration complexity and insufficient interdisciplinary validation. Future research should establish standardized evaluation frameworks to advance game design from entertainment-focused application toward broader social demands including education and health care.

records.title: A team approach to teaching molecular biosciences: involving, recognising and rewarding others
records.abstract: In many areas of academia, there is a tradition of individual excellence. Often we attribute a discovery or innovation to a particular person, rather than including the researchers under their supervision. Individuals may also be promoted through Senior Lecturer, Reader, Professor, etc. for their academic pursuits without rewarding the collaborating staff and students who also contributed. Indeed, prizes are often awarded for the impact purported to emanate from a single person rather than the teams they work within or co-ordinate.In many ways, this does not reflect the way academia actually operates or at least not the optimal ways of working which bring the most value to research, teaching and external engagement within universities. One could imagine, for example, lecturers believing that their individual excellence means that, although they feel they should teach, constitutes an excellent educational experience for students. This may even be done without consulting the latest pedagogical advances and evidence that could help them improve. Equally problematic might be a personal tutor or academic advisor who believes their individual excellence will help them solve a student’s mental health issue rather than involving the appropriate, specialist services.I believe that bringing in others and harnessing their expertise is how I have been able to make the greatest advances. Because of this, I maintain that championing their contributions is of great importance in encouraging a steer away from a fixation on individual excellence and towards a culture of collaborative working. As such, in this article, I hope to shed some light on the different collaborators I have in higher education, how they have effected change and how I have attempted to reward and recognise them for their efforts in this area.During my time at the university, I have worked with a wide variety of taught students in various ways and across a multitude of areas. In fact, my own journey in teaching started as a Peer-assisted Study Session (PASS) Leader, working collaboratively with another 2nd-year Molecular Biologist to look after a group of new 1st-year Life Science students. We were trained in the facilitation of learning and encouraged to stimulate conversation and interaction between the students rather than to act as expert instructors, so as not to attempt to replicate or even duplicate the work of the lecturers on the course.Fast forward 9 years, I find myself in the lecturing position, introducing flipped learning into my course modules by moving content delivery from the on-campus sessions to streamlined learning outcome-focussed videos. This did, however, leave me with an issue: I now had hours’ worth of contact time with the students that I needed to do something with. My first thought was to write lots of practice questions myself, but then I began to wonder if I was the best placed person to be doing this. I could probably come up with areas that I assume the students would find most challenging and design questions that I think they might find useful. But, why do all the guesswork when there were students in later years who had already done the unit and knew exactly what would have been helpful? Furthermore, many of these students had gone on to become PASS Leaders themselves giving them a dual expertise in the student experience of the course and facilitating active learning.By involving these students in the design of synchronous formative assessment of learning activities, we were able to harness the experience of looking back on the course as a whole, knowledge of creating interactive learning environments and subject expertise as a team. It has also become a collaborative and iterative way of refreshing the course each year, with new cohorts of unit alumni providing more exercises. This also allows a bank of old archived exercises from previous years to be provided as extra learning resources.Additionally, my reviewing of the in-class questions designed each year allows me to reflect on my own part of the learning process. An example of this is as follows: when PASS Leaders create questions that do not test the intended learning outcomes of the course, I am made aware of my own shortcomings in articulating clearly what students need to be able to do. The creation of formative exercises by the higher year students for use in my courses is invaluable in terms of the improvements that can be made each year and the enhanced learning of those currently on the course in getting the practice and feedback they find most useful.Many programmes offer a capstone project or similar piece of work that allows taught students to bring together the various parts of their degree learning up to that point. In some areas, this project can be related to the teaching of the subject area being studied, rather than undertaking practical assignments in the discipline. My involvement in this form of education was, interestingly, in the year after I had started to introduce flipped learning approaches to my courses when I was asked if I could provide a project for a group of 3rd years. I was initially at a loss being teaching-focussed and having neither biochemical nor pedagogical research to speak of. However, I reflected on the learning journey I had been through in creating video content for my modules and thought that this would be a great experience for undergraduate students. As such, I designed a project whereby the project group would create a cohesive online course comprising audio-visual material, online assessments and any extra reading or materials that might be of use. Altogether the course would need to be coherent, but each group member could take the lead on a submodule. For the literature review component, the students would need to consult science education and e-learning articles, as I did before with my own course design efforts, to identify effective practices in creating flipped learning materials.As the students were given the freedom to choose what they wanted their online course to be about, they chose something to help earlier year students with an aspect of the curriculum. This meant that, with the creators’ permission, the resources could be provided to future students for their benefit, including some being embedded directly into courses. It was great to see how the project students drew on different parts of the course, such as the science communication module in 2nd year and various parts of the subject content delivery along with their newly learned educational knowledge from the current literature. The fact that it was their own subject knowledge and new content from the literature review meant that there was no reason why the groups had to be made up of students from the same subject. This opened up the possibility of having a group where the members were from various degree programmes, learning the teaching and theories together through their literature review and then bringing their degree-specific knowledge to creation of their specific module. As such, in subsequent years, there were educational project groups that included chemists, mathematicians and engineers working together to produce digital learning materials. In these cases, it was evident that the students learnt from each other’s knowledge, incorporating concepts and case studies from other discipline areas. Examples of how this content was then used for student benefit include videos and practice tests on mathematical concepts that underpin computational modules being included in Natural Science modules.The students who contributed to either synchronous exercises or asynchronous video and quiz content were, of course, recognised through official channels. For PASS Leaders, they received recognition on their Higher Education Achievement Record, and for educational project students, there were the credits gained through doing the group project. However, it was evident to me that the reward was different from what would be granted to a member of staff doing the same work. For example, new lecturers often submit their course design work as a portfolio to achieve accreditation by Advance HE. In the interests of parity of esteem, I set out to see if something similar might be possible for taught students.Reviewing what was then the relevant UK Professional Standards Framework for teaching and supporting learning in higher education, I could see that the activities fit well. Both sets of students had demonstrated they could “design and plan learning activities...” and “engage in continuing professional development in subjects/disciplines and their pedagogy, incorporating research [and] scholarship...” They could also demonstrate knowledge of “the subject material” and “appropriate methods for teaching, learning and assessing in the subject area and at the level of the academic programme”, as well as a commitment to “appropriate professional values”. As such, all of those involved who applied to become Associate Fellows of the Higher Education Academy (AFHEA) were successful. It was fantastic to see students rewarded commensurately as higher education professionals and the effect this had on their future applications to become secondary school teachers or graduate teaching assistants through further study at university. Their applications are also now used as exemplars across the university to support the taught student pathway to accreditation, which has been opened up to everyone who contributes to learning support at the institution.This section is written by Dr. Mauro Adriel Rinaldi: former Postdoc and Teaching Assistant on Dr. Weise’s student co-created course.Many university lecturers transition from postdoctoral research roles (PDRAs), often with limited formal teaching experience. While PDRAs may mentor or train colleagues in the lab, these activities rarely equip them with the pedagogical tools needed for effective classroom teaching. This leaves them at a disadvantage, especially when transitioning into academic roles with significant teaching responsibilities.PDRAs fall through a gap between graduate teaching assistants, who get training, and new academics. Teaching experience is crucial for their career progression, helping them secure lectureships and refine their skills before taking on the heavy responsibilities of leading courses. However, many PDRAs struggle to access teaching opportunities due to role constraints or supervisors prioritising research output.When integrated into teaching, PDRAs offer immense value. They facilitate research-informed teaching through their up-to-date perspectives of the field, empathise with student challenges and act as a direct link to lab-based learning. Programmes like the Teaching for Researchers course at the University of Manchester address this gap by providing monthly sessions over a year on pedagogy, reflection and classroom techniques. This incremental approach allows PDRAs to balance professional development with research, fostering sustained growth and confidence as educators.Participating in Nick’s flipped course gave me a low-pressure environment to learn pedagogy. Watching students engage with pre-recorded materials and guiding them through practical exercises sharpened my teaching skills and provided valuable insights into student learning. Encouraged to admit when we didn’t know an answer, we could focus on fostering critical thinking and facilitating problem-solving, creating impactful moments where students gained confidence through their own efforts.Presenting in class further allowed me to refine my teaching style, balancing the students’ learning outcomes with my development goals. These experiences are unusual for PDRAs and prepared me for future challenges, offering a gradual introduction to teaching responsibilities.The support of a teaching community was instrumental in my growth. Initiatives like pedagogy journal clubs, mentorship programmes and the Chemistry Postdoctoral Society provided spaces to share experiences and learn collaboratively. These networks fostered reflective practice, helping me approach teaching with greater confidence and adaptability. So, the team approach is wider than just the lecturer–PDRA relationship.Inspired by Nick’s teaching, I invited eight speakers from business development, industry, government agencies, technology support organisations and academic research into my Biotechnology module in my role as Lecturer, benefiting all involved, and will continue to build on this team approach to teaching.Higher Education Academy (HEA) accreditation programmes formalised our contributions, bolstering our identities as educators and overcoming impostor syndrome. Many PDRAs went on to lectureships, forming a nationwide network of connected teaching professionals that continues to share insights and strengthen academic practices.Recognition, importantly, flows both ways. I nominated Nick for the Biochemical Society Teaching Excellence Award to acknowledge his pivotal role in my development. Nick also applied for and obtained a high commendation for Inclusive Education and Flexible Learning and Digital Delivery from the University of Manchester Teaching Excellence Awards for the Industrial Biotechnology Team, further validating our collective efforts. His reciprocal recognition of my contributions reinforced the value of teamwork and mutual appreciation, fostering a culture that celebrates collective success over individual accolades.Based on the experiences recounted in this article, below are some top tips and ideas that can be considered for those teaching in the area of biochemistry (and more widely):Involving students as co-creators in educational activities not only enhances their learning experience but also provides lecturers with valuable feedback to continuously refine their teaching practices. Educational projects and flipped learning methods further demonstrate the power of student contributions, blending subject knowledge with innovative pedagogical tools to benefit future cohorts. Recognising students through formal pathways, such as Associate Fellowship accreditation, not only motivates them but also prepares them for impactful careers in academia and beyond.Similarly, integrating postdoctoral researchers into teaching roles creates a dual benefit: enriching the learning experience for students while equipping PDRAs with the skills and confidence to excel as future educators. Programmes like Teaching for Researchers exemplify how structured support, reflection and accreditation can transform early-career researchers into effective teachers, fostering a network of teaching professionals that transcends institutional boundaries.A team-based approach to teaching, as illustrated by the examples in this article, champions the value of collaboration, mutual recognition and shared achievements. Shifting the focus from individual excellence to collective success not only strengthens academic culture but also nurtures a supportive, inclusive environment where everyone—from students to staff—can thrive. Recognising and rewarding the contributions of all collaborators is not just an ethical imperative but a necessary step toward a more sustainable and impactful academic system.By fostering these values, we can create a legacy of shared learning and growth that benefits both individuals and institutions, ultimately advancing the field of molecular biosciences and academia as a whole.Nick Weise is a Principal Fellow of the Higher Education Academy holding joint Senior Lectureships in the Manchester Institute of Biotechnology and Manchester Medical School. He is also Faculty Lead for Student Engagement & Inclusion (Biology, Medicine & Health) and Departmental Lead for Teaching & Learning Enhancement (Chemistry) at the University of Manchester. He obtained a BSc in Molecular Biology before undertaking a PhD in Chemistry & Biochemistry and subsequently working as a Public Engagement Programme Manager. He then received his current academic position in 2017 and was promoted in 2022. Email: nicholas.weise@manchester.ac.uk.Dr Mauro Adriel Rinaldi is a Lecturer in Biotechnology and Biochemistry at University of Hull specialising in synthetic organelles for biomanufacturing. With a passion for innovative pedagogy, he has delivered active learning strategies, interdisciplinary teaching, and the professional development of early-career researchers, becoming a Senior Fellow of the Higher Education Academy. His work integrates teaching and research, offering students opportunities to engage with cutting-edge topics in biotechnology. Drawing on his experience at Rice University, The University of Manchester and University of York, Dr. Rinaldi’s collaborative teaching approach fosters student success while advancing the field of sustainable chemical production. Email: M.Rinaldi@hull.ac.uk.

records.title: AATransID : enhancing cross-domain person re-identification with low-rank adaptation and sequence sampling
records.venue: International Journal of Multimedia Information Retrieval
records.abstract: Person re-identification (ReID) is a pivotal task in computer vision, aiming to match individuals across non-overlapping camera views. Despite significant advancements, current ReID methodologies often suffer from limited generalization capabilities, especially in cross-domain scenarios where training and testing datasets differ in environments, camera settings, and appearance variations. To address these challenges, we propose AATransID, a novel person ReID model based on a pure Vision Transformer architecture. We introduce a sequence sampling methodology that acts as an effective regularization technique, exposing the model to a wide range of intra-class variations and temporal contexts, thereby enhancing its robustness. Additionally, we integrate ArcFace loss with triplet loss to refine the feature space. With low-rank adaptation, AATransID achieves substantial improvements in mean average precision (mAP) on multiple benchmark datasets, surpassing existing state-of-the-art models by 4.8% on Market-1501, 1.6% on DukeMTMC-reID, 7.7% on MSMT17, and 2.2% on Occluded-Duke. Source code is available at https://github.com/serdaryildiz/AATransID.

records.title: ABSTRACT NUMBER: ESOC2026A2387 UNDERSTANDING TASK CHALLENGE IN STROKE REHABILITATION TO SUPPORT OPERATIONALISATION: AN INTERDISCIPLINARY CONCEPT ANALYSIS
records.abstract: Abstract Background and aims Task challenge is widely recognised as fundamental to effective stroke rehabilitation, yet is inconsistently defined, operationalised, and reported. This conceptual ambiguity limits intervention design, replication, and evidence synthesis, and understanding of dose–response relationships in stroke recovery. We aimed to clarify how task challenge is conceptualised in stroke rehabilitation research and to provide a framework to support future operationalisation and evaluation. Methods We undertook a principle-based interdisciplinary concept analysis. A mulit-database systematic search identified peer-reviewed literature addressing task challenge or related constructs in stroke rehabilitation research literature. Forty-two papers were purposively selected for high informational value. Guided by epistemological, pragmatic, linguistic, and logical principles, we used iterative immersion, analytical questioning, coding, constant comparison, and synthesis to identify antecedents, defining attributes, and outcomes of task challenge. Results Task challenge was conceptualised as a multifaceted, multidimensional, and dynamic interaction between the task, the person’s ability, and their subjective experience. Three interrelated facets were identified: nominal challenge (task demands), functional challenge (demands relative to ability), and perceived challenge (experienced effort or difficulty). Functional and perceived challenge were central to optimal challenge, and associated with enhanced recovery, engagement, and positive emotional responses after stroke. Across disciplines, challenge was rarely explicitly defined, and inconsistent terminology reduced conceptual clarity and reporting precision. Conclusions This analysis provides a stroke-specific conceptual framework of task challenge. Clarifying its multifaceted, multidimensional, and dynamic nature provides a foundation to support future operationalisation, improve intervention design and reporting, and enable more precise investigation of dose–response mechanisms in stroke rehabilitation trials. records.abstract: ASTHI-DM: A SIMPLE, CLINICAL RISK SCORE FOR FRACTURE RISK STRATIFICATION IN TYPE 2 DIABETES IN RESOURCE-LIMITED SETTINGS *Lakshmi Nagendra, Rayeerth Dasgupta, Gargi Banerjee, Riddhi Dasgupta JSS Medical College, JSS Academy of Higher Education and Research, Mysore, Karnataka, India *E-mail: [email protected] Introduction: Individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) have a disproportionately high risk of fragility fractures that is poorly captured by conventional bone mineral density-based approaches. Fracture risk assessment in diabetes commonly relies on dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) and trabecular bone score (TBS). However, access to DXA and TBS remains limited across many low- and middle-income countries, constraining their usefulness for population-level screening and routine diabetes care. Scalable, imaging-independent strategies are therefore urgently needed. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study of 263 adults with T2DM undergoing evaluation for bone health. The primary outcome was prevalent fragility fractures. Multiple supervised machine learning models were developed using routinely available demographic, clinical, and biochemical variables. Parallel analyses were performed with and without inclusion of TBS to assess dependence on advanced skeletal imaging. Based on the stability of SHapley Additive exPlanations-identified predictors and consistent performance across TBS-inclusive and TBS-exclusive models, penalized regression was employed to derive a parsimonious, interpretable fracture risk score. Results: The final ASTHI-DM score comprised five routinely available clinical variables: age ≥70 years, female gender, low body weight (<60 kg), history of falls or chronic systemic glucocorticoid exposure, and adverse skeletal history. Each variable was assigned 2 points, yielding a total score range of 0–10 points. Patients were stratified into low- (0–3 points), moderate- (4–7 points), and high-risk (≥8 points) categories. Fracture prevalence increased progressively across these tiers (4.0%, 21.3%, and 50.0%, respectively), demonstrating a clear dose–response relationship and supporting the construct validity of the score. At a lower threshold of ≥4 points, the score demonstrated high sensitivity (91.9%) and negative predictive value (96.4%), making it well suited for screening and risk exclusion in routine diabetes clinics. In contrast, a higher threshold of ≥8 points substantially improved specificity (95.2%) and positive predictive value (50.0%), albeit with reduced sensitivity, thereby enriching for individuals at particularly high fracture risk. Conclusion: ASTHI-DM offers a simple, low-cost, imaging-independent approach to fracture risk stratification in T2DM. By eliminating dependence on DXA and TBS, this tool is well suited for implementation in resource-limited settings. ASTHI-DM has potential to support equitable fracture risk identification. ASSESSMENT OF NEUROCOGNITIVE FUNCTION IN TYPE 2 DIABETES INDIAN PATIENTS AND ASSOCIATED CLINICO-BIOCHEMICAL PARAMETERS – AN ANALYTICAL OBSERVATIONAL STUDY *Mukesh Darshan, Manisha Naithani AIIMS, Rishikesh, Uttarakhand, India *E-mail: [email protected] Introduction: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is one of the major causes of increasing morbidity worldwide. Effective screening is carried out routinely for diabetes retinopathy, neuropathy, and nephropathy. Of late, studies have reported that cognitive decline can occur in people with diabetes which could go undetected for a long period and therefore routine screening is warranted. Methods: Our objective was to study the prevalence of previously unknown cognitive impairment (CI) in type 2 diabetes patients visiting a tertiary care center with the Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination (ACE) score and to study the correlations of hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), fasting blood sugar (FBS), postprandial blood sugar (PPBS), age, and duration of diabetes with the ACE scores. One hundred and ninety-three patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus were included in the study. Patients with ACE scores ≥88 were considered to have normal cognition (NC) and those with <88 CI. Additionally, among CI diabetes patients, levels of C-reactive protein, tumor necrosis factor-alpha), and interleukin-6 were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay techniques to look for correlation. Results: CI was noted in 30 (15.5%) type 2 diabetes mellitus patients. Those with CI had higher HbA1c (9.79 ± 1.85 vs. 7.72 ± 1.60), higher FBS (197.05 ± 62.48 vs. 139.38 ± 54.38), and PPBS (292.03 ± 75.61 vs. 204.50 ± 62.43), which were statistically significant. The cognitive domains of attention, memory, language, and visuospatial abilities showed a statistically significant difference between those with CI and NC. The levels of inflammatory markers were increased among CI diabetes patients, which were statistically significant. Various factors such as diabetes duration of more than 10 years, presence of microvascular disease, smoking, concurrent hypertension, and history of self-reported hypoglycemia were found to be significantly associated with CI. The mean level of inflammatory markers was found to be lower in cases of associated factors such as insulin use, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor use, and Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitor/ Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARB) use among CI diabetes patients. Conclusion: The prevalence of CI in type 2 diabetes patients highlights the importance of implementing routine cognitive testing. The association between CI and inflammatory pathway and predictive role needs further research. records.abstract: Female sexual interest/arousal disorder: Rethinking diagnosis, distress, and cultural blind spots in India Aakanksha Malhotra, Anita Shyam, Siddharth Chowdhury, Sourav Bag Female Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder (FSIAD), as described in the DSM-5-TR, involves a persistent reduction in sexual interest, fantasy, initiation, receptivity, or arousal that results in clinically significant distress. In Indian clinical settings, FSIAD is shaped by a multifactorial interplay of neurobiology, the female sexual response cycle, relationship dynamics, trauma histories, sociocultural expectations, and chronic stress. These influences are particularly pronounced in contexts where silence, shame, and marital obligation shape women’s sexual experiences. This workshop reframes FSIAD through an integrative, culturally grounded lens. Participants will learn to differentiate between low desire, suppressed desire, context-dependent desire, and trauma-related shutdown—distinctions crucial for accurate diagnosis and compassionate care. The session blends clinical science, the sexual response cycle, culturally sensitive interviewing, and practical management strategies relevant to psychiatric and sexual-medicine practice in India. A key component of the workshop is demonstration of Somatic bodywork Principles,sensate-focus principles, illustrating how clinicians can help patients rebuild sensory awareness, reduce performance pressure, and cultivate non-goal-directed intimacy. Through structured assessment pathways and evidence-informed interventions, the workshop equips clinicians to deliver nuanced, ethical, and contextually meaningful sexual healthcare to women in India. Implementation research for mental health disorders Abhishek Ghosh, Arpit Parmar1, Shankar Prinja2, R. Johnson Pradeep3, Pulkit Verma4, Neha Dahiya5, Ashok Grover5 Department of Psychiatry, Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER), 2Department of Community Medicine, School of Public Health, Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER), Chandigarh, 1Department of Psychiatry, All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Bhubaneswar, Odisha, 3Department of Psychiatry, St. John’s Medical College, Bengaluru, Karnataka, 4Division of Non-Communicable Diseases, Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), 5Division of Implementation Research, Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), New Delhi, India Implementation research (IR) bridges the gap by evaluating strategies to integrate evidence-based mental health interventions into real-world systems at scale, with fidelity, equity, and efficiency. This 3-hour workshop introduces core IR concepts and frameworks within India’s policy and funding landscape, specifically the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) prioritization of IR and current exemplars. Participants will learn to frame IR questions; select and apply determinant, process, and outcome frameworks (e.g., CFIR, TIDieR, RE-AIM, Proctor outcomes); design feasible hybrid effectiveness-implementation studies; and plan pragmatic measurement. A dedicated segment demystifies economic evaluation in IR, covering costing approaches (ingredients/micro-costing), cost-benefit/utility/effectiveness distinctions, perspective, time horizon, and budget-impact analysis tailored to public programs. The workshop concludes with a step-by-step walkthrough of the ICMR-MINDS study, integrating mental and substance-use care into NCD services. Using ICMR-MINDS as a prototype, faculty will illustrate co-design with health systems, selection of implementation strategies (ERIC), choice of outcomes (acceptability, feasibility, fidelity, penetration, sustainability), data systems, and economic analyses aligned to decision-makers’ needs. Participants will draft a one-page IR protocol on a mental health integration issue in small groups, with real-time faculty feedback. By the end, attendees will leave with (i) a practical checklist for planning IR, (ii) templated tools (problem statement â†’ logic model â†’ framework selection â†’ outcomes â†’ costing plan), and (iii) an understanding of how to align proposals with ICMR priorities and funder expectations. The workshop targets clinicians, public-health practitioners, early-career investigators, program managers, and policymakers seeking to move beyond efficacy to scalable, sustainable mental-health care. Sensory, structure, safety: A framework for sexuality in neurodivergence Anita Shyam, Siddharth Chowdhury RxMen/Psymantra Institute Private Limited, Dhampur, Uttar Pradesh, India Psychosexual medicine has historically centred on neurotypical assumptions of desire, arousal, and intimacy. Emerging evidence in ADHD, autism spectrum conditions, and learning differences reveals distinct sensory, cognitive, and relational mechanisms that influence sexual functioning. Current Indian practice seldom accounts for these profiles, leading to misdiagnosis, over-pathologisation, and therapeutic blind spots. This workshop introduces a neurodivergent-affirmative clinical framework, Sensory, Structure, Safety, that reconceptualises sexual health assessment and therapy for minds wired differently. Through brief didactics, live case demonstrations, and interactive exercises, facilitators will: (1) map neurobiological and sensory determinants of sexual behaviour in neurodivergent adults; (2) identify patterns of hyper and hyposexuality, rejection sensitivity, and executive-function impact; (3) demonstrate adapted interviewing, psychoeducation, and therapeutic strategies; and (4) examine ethical, cultural, and consent issues specific to Indian psychiatry. Participants will acquire a ready-to-use clinical grid integrating sensory processing, structural predictability, and safety calibration into psychosexual formulation. The session challenges prevailing reductionist models and advocates an inclusive standard for sexual-health care in neurodivergent populations. Connecting with confidence – How to master your 7-minute pitch Astha, Sachin Gandotra, Jatinder Kour, Swapnil Yadav, Baxi Neeraj Prasad Sinha Tees Esk and Wear Valley NHS Trust, Middlesbrough, United Kingdom While education in psychiatry is undergoing a transformative reform, interviewing patients in a clinical setting has been essential. The clinical interview is central in psychiatry: it’s how you build rapport, while gaining leads from (gather) the history, understand the person’s experience and guides towards formulation of a working diagnosis and plan. Good interviewing improves diagnostic accuracy, therapeutic relationship and patient outcomes (and reduces patient distress). Interviewing in psychiatry has additional layers (mental state, risk, subjective experiences, stigma) compared with non-psychiatric settings, so the skills need more emphasis.Reflective listening, empathy and adequate pauses can help in maintaining a flow of conversations. The core elements of interview that the workshop aims to focus on : 1 Setting the scene 2. Opening the interview 3. History taking 4. Collaborative plan. The workshop aims to give a simulated and a learning experience with a role player/actor and a psychiatrist conducting the interview of different clinical scenarios in the format as guided by the international academic organisations. This workshop aims to target early career psychiatrists who are exploring different career pathways. 6th National Official Workshop on Technology and Futuristic Psychiatry by IPS Technology and Psychiatry Subcommittee Darpan Kaur, Mary Dsouza, Rajiv Saini, Sandeep Vohra Consultant Psychiatrst There is perceived need to upskill psychiatrists in technology and futuristic psychiatry. We will conduct the 6th National Official Workshop of IPS Technology & Psychiatry Subcommittee at ANCIPS, 2026. The prescriber’s paradox: Art and science of psychopharmacology in the elderly Debanjan Banerjee, Anwesak Das1, Nahid Islam2 Apollo Multispecialty Hospitals, Kolkata, West Bengal, 1Health City Hospital, 2GNRC Hospitals, Guwahati, Assam, India Psychopharmacology in older adults presents one of the most nuanced challenges in contemporary psychiatry. The ageing brain, altered pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, multimorbidity, and polypharmacy create a delicate balance between therapeutic benefit and potential harm - what may be lifesaving in midlife can be disabling in late life. This workshop explores the intricate interface between evidence and individualization, where science meets clinical intuition. Through a series of interactive, case-based discussions, participants will engage with real-world dilemmas that mirror day-to-day geriatric psychiatric practice ranging from antidepressant selection in frailty and managing agitation in dementia, to deprescribing long-term benzodiazepines. The focus will be on rational prescribing, minimizing drug- drug interactions, and recognizing the art of deprescribing as a therapeutic act.Three experienced clinicians will jointly lead the session, integrating pharmacological principles with ethical reasoning, person-centred care, and practical tips for optimising treatment safety. Audience participation, small-group problem solving, and consensus reflection will ensure applied learning rather than theoretical review.Ultimately, the workshop aims to equip participants with confidence to navigate the paradox of geriatric psychopharmacology to know when to prescribe, how to individualize, and when to stop. Stimulating clarity: Practical tDCS masterclass for cognitive and affective disorders in late life Debanjan Banerjee, Sachin Arora1, Vishal Chhabra2 Apollo Multispecialty Hospitals, Kolkata, West Bengal, 1Consultant Psychiatrist, 2Chhabra Psychiatry Centre and Fortis Hospital, Vasant Kunj, New Delhi, India Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS) has emerged as a safe, portable, and affordable neuromodulatory technique with increasing relevance in old age psychiatry, particularly for disorders involving cognitive decline, affective dysregulation, and inadequate response to conventional treatments. With India’s rapidly ageing population and the rising burden of dementia and late-life depression, clinicians require practical skills to apply tDCS effectively and safely in older adults. Although tDCS appears simple in principle, its clinical success depends on choosing the right indications, understanding electrode montages, optimizing current intensity and session scheduling, and carefully monitoring elderly patients with multimorbidity. This workshop offers a hands-on, skill-based training experience conducted by three practising psychiatry consultants experienced in neuromodulation and geriatric mental health. Participants will learn step-by-step tDCS administration techniques, including preparation, electrode placement, device calibration, and management of common technical and clinical pitfalls. records.abstract: Poster #101 Debriefing Post Codes to Improve Teamwork Behaviors in Real Life Cardiopulmonary Arrest Events Presentation Category: Debriefing Tara Mahramus, MSN, CNS, CCRN, CCNS,1 Mai Vo, MD,1 Mindi Anderson, PhD, ARNP, CPNP-PC, CHSE-A,2 Daleen Penoyer, PhD, RN, CCRP, FCCM1 1ORLANDO HEALTH, ORLANDO, FLORIDA, UNITED STATES; 2ORLANDO HEALTH AND UNIVERSITY OF CENTRAL FLORIDA, ORLANDO, FLORIDA, UNITED STATES Introduction: Debriefing is an interactive learning process that provides opportunity for teams to reflect upon their actions, performance and thought processes after an event.1,2 Debriefings are used in healthcare after cardiopulmonary arrest (CPA) events to improve communication, leadership, and situational awareness.1,2,3 Despite the value of debriefs, they are often not done.4 At the study site, baseline debriefings post CPA events were documented only 3% of the time. A meta-analysis revealed that individual and team performances improved by 25% when debriefings were done post events.2 This prompted the investigators to test an intervention of training a group of interprofessional resuscitation responders to do structured debriefings after real life CPA events. Research questions for the study were: Does an educational intervention and implementation of post-CPA debriefing process improve interprofessional teamwork performance in real life CPA events, impact team members’ perception of post-CPA debriefings, and increase the number of documented debriefings? Methods: A prospective, before-and-after quasi-experimental, mixed methods design was used for this study. Teamwork was assessed using a validated TEAM tool.5 Baseline TEAM tool5 data was collected for two months pre study to measure teamwork perceptions of responders to CPA events. A one-time educational debriefing intervention was offered three times for team members (n=47). The intervention included education on principles of teamwork behaviors, debriefing components, and exercises for role play of debriefing after simulated CPA events. Participants were assigned various roles during to gain experience as debriefing leader or team member, modeled some after a presentation by Onello et al.6 After the education intervention, attendees were asked to perform debriefings post real life CPA events, document debriefing done on the CPA audit, and complete the TEAM tool5. TEAM tool5 data was collected for eight months after the debriefing education. Data from CPA audits were analyzed to determine debriefing occurrence. Subjects were given three open-ended questions about their experience with debriefing. Results: One hundred sixty three team members participated in the pre and post TEAM assessments: 62% RNs, 15% (RTs), 4% nursing assistants, 16% physicians, and 3% pharmacists. Thirty team members completed TEAM assessments in 5 CPA events pre-intervention and 133 in 19 CPA events post-intervention. Experience ranged from <1-40 years; the majority with 1-5 years (71%). A significant difference in demographics between years of experience pre and post intervention (9.9 vs. 7.3, p=0.004). Most CPA events were on step down units (39%), followed by 28% in critical care. TEAM5 scores did not significantly differ between the pre- and post-debriefing intervention (48.6 vs. 48.9, p=0.89). Post hoc analysis showed a significant difference in task management scores between pharmacists and RTs. No differences in scores found between disciplines, experience, or unit where CPA occurred. Post-CPA debriefings increased from 3% to 11% during the intervention period. Themes from qualitative remarks of team members who participated in a debriefing post CPA event were identifying opportunities for improvement, communication, and team functioning. Conclusion: While no significant differences were found in teamwork scores before and after the debriefing intervention, we found that team members valued debriefings after codes and found them beneficial to detect opportunities for improvement, communication, and team functioning. It is possible the TEAM tool5 was not a valid measure for improvements in team functioning related to increased performance of debriefings. A convenience sample of team members who participated in the evaluations regardless if they participated in the education intervention or if a debriefing was done at the CPA event attended may be limitations. This may have also influenced their TEAM tool5 scores. However, we believe the TEAM tool5 may be useful in evaluating teamwork in real life CPA events where all subjects attend the debriefing education class and participate in a debriefing post CPA. Team members valued debriefings and a marked improvement in the number of debriefings post-CPA events was seen after emphasis on this type of intervention. Simulation-based learning is composed of three steps: prebriefing, simulation experience, and debriefing. During debriefing, learners reflect on the simulation experience using metacognitive strategies under the guidance of an instructor who provides the learners with feedback on actual performance, factual errors, and cognitive reconstruction. Students benefit from debriefing activities in simulation-based education, by discovering their mistakes and learning how to correct them. It is felt that there is a critical need to develop standardized debriefing guidelines and evaluation models for more effective debriefing activities. This could be standardized guidelines and approaches to simulated education. The purpose of this study was to identify how debriefing was practiced in simulation-based nursing education in Korea in order to provide basic information for the development of more standardized debriefing guidelines in simulation-based nursing education in Korea. records.title: ABSTRACTS: Abstracts of Papers Presented at the 53rd Annual Scientific Meeting of the Association for Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback
records.abstract: The 53rd Annual Scientific Meeting of the Association for Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback (AAPB) was held at the Caribe Royale Hotel in Orlando, Florida. The theme of the meeting was ‘‘Training the Injured Brain with Biofeedback and Neurofeedback.’’ The meeting included diverse program offerings and a full array of exhibits as well as 9 preconference workshops, 26 breakout sessions, 3 oral presentations, 2 Lunch-and-Learn sessions, and 22 poster presentations. Keynote presentations were provided by Bruno Demichelis, PhD; Inna Khazan, PhD, BCB, BCB-HRV; and Ruth Lanius, MD, PhD. Stephen W. Porges, PhD, delivered the Distinguished Scientist Lecture. The 2023 Program Committee was chaired by Inna Khazan, PhD, BCB, BCB-HRV.The 54th Annual Meeting will be held May 8–11, 2024, at the Hyatt Regency DTC in Denver, Colorado.Heart rate variability (HRV) has been a focal point throughout my academic history. For perspective, I have published studies focusing on HRV, spanning seven decades (1969–2022). My interest in HRV started early in graduate school and continues to be an important portal to inform my theoretical perspective. The presentation will track this history, which started as an empirical observation and moved through several scientific stages, including the development of quantitative methods and investigations of neural mechanisms. Along this journey, a variety of hypotheses were tested, including the relative sensitivity of HRV metrics to neural mechanisms, psychological processes, and medical diagnoses. In addition, the research led to the identification of portals of intervention that have become strategies by which to optimize mental and physical health. These apparently disparate programs of inquiry have been tightly merged as the Polyvagal Theory has evolved. The presentation will share my personal journey through these stages of scientific inquiry and my attempts to integrate the new knowledge into an expansive theoretical model.Correspondence: Stephen W. Porges, PhD, Indiana University Bloomington & University of North Carolina Chapel Hill, sporges@gmail.comThis session aims to offer a working framework (a map of meaning) that combines Dr. Demichelis’ practical experience and data collected over the span of 20 years with his stress assessment. When we navigate complex realities, such as performance enhancement, human development, and peak performance, we need a solid paradigm in order to be able to make informed decisions and design protocols. During this session, we will review a summary of the psychophysiological profile of the peak performer and review some of the seven components of Dr. Demichelis’ framework.Bruno Demichelis, PhD, Private Practice/Sport Psychology, hello@thelabofmeditation.comIn a field as versatile and diverse as biofeedback, best practices are sometimes intertwined with myths and misconceptions. In this talk, we will discuss some of the common myths and misconceptions about various aspects of biofeedback, common mistakes that decrease biofeedback efficacy, and ways to address them in biofeedback practice. This talk is grounded in research in psychophysiology, mindfulness, and self-compassion.Correspondence: Inna Khazan, PhD, BCB, BCB-HRV, Harvard Medical School, inna.khazan@gmail.comElectroencephalogram (EEG) neurofeedback, which is aimed at reducing the amplitude of the alpha-rhythms in the brain, has been shown to alter critical brain networks that are associated with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), resulting in symptom alleviation among individuals with PTSD. A recent randomized controlled trial has shown that alpha neurofeedback can lead to clinically meaningful reductions in PTSD symptoms. The mechanism underlying these neuroplastic changes of alpha neurofeedback are beginning to be revealed and will be discussed during this keynote lecture. Moreover, the application of this type of neurofeedback in patients with complex trauma and dissociative symptomatology will be illustrated through case examples. Finally, combining alpha neurofeedback with traditional Indigenous practices will be described as a means of addressing the intergenerational transmission of trauma in this population.Correspondence: Ruth Lanius, MD, PhD, Western University of Canada, Ruth.lanius@lhsc.on.caPhotobiomodulation (PBM) is a non-invasive and innovative treatment approach that leverages light therapy to stimulate cells and tissues at a cellular level by using near-infrared (NIR) and infrared (IR) light. First, this presentation will discuss the mechanics of PBM, including the differences between NIR and IR wavelengths as well as their skin penetration rates. The role of nanometers in PBM will also be explored. Second, the biological effects of PBM will be covered, including its impact on mitochondria, neuron excitotoxicity, synaptogenesis, angiogenesis, blood flow, inflammation, apoptosis, neuron progenitor cells, antioxidants, and neurotrophies. Third, this presentation will discuss the application of PBM in treating various brain disorders, including anxiety, depression, Alzheimer’s Disease, and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Last, a case study of a 32-year-old female suffering from postpartum depression will be presented as an example of the clinical application of PBM. Overall, this abstract provides a comprehensive overview of PBM and its potential therapeutic benefits in treating brain disorders.Correspondence: Rebekah Walker, iMediSync, rebekah@imedisync.comTreating a severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) requires the use of a multimodal approach under the guise of inpatient rehabilitation. However, once inpatient rehabilitation has been terminated due to a lack of further progress, what options do patients have? The patient sustained a closed-head left temporal injury with coup contrecoup impact to the frontal region. The patient underwent a left side craniotomy and was comatose for 26 days. records.abstract: THE EFFECT OF KINESIOTAPE® IN COMBINATION WITH SUPRAMALLEOLAR ORTHOTICS VERSUS ANKLE FOOT ORTHOTICS ON BALANCE AND FUNCTION IN A CHILD WITH CEREBRAL PALSY Booth J. Quinnipiac University. Hamden, CT. BACKGROUND & PURPOSE: Research has been limited in the area of Kinesiotape® (KT), specifically in the pediatric population with cerebral palsy (CP). Often children diagnosed with CP who have gait and balance deficits are prescribed orthotics. While these orthoses may improve foot position and stability, they also inhibit normal joint mechanics. The purpose of this case study was to investigate the effect of Kinesiotaping® for functional dorsiflexion in combination with supramalleolar orthotics (SMO) versus ankle foot orthotics (AFO) on balance and function in a child with spastic diplegic CP. CASE DESCRIPTION: The participant was an eight-year-old male diagnosed with spastic diplegic CP who ambulated independently with and without the aid of bilateral AFOs. He presented with increased tone and decreased strength in his bilateral ankle plantar flexors and dorsiflexors. The participant was evaluated under 3 conditions; barefoot, with AFOs, and with KT for functional bilateral ankle dorsiflexion combined with SMOs. The Pediatric Balance Scale (PBS) and the Timed-up-and-go (TUG) test were used to evaluate the participant under all three conditions twice per week for four-weeks. OUTCOMES: The Friedman's test followed by a Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test was used to compare all data collected. A Bonferroni correction was applied resulting in a new p-value of p = 0.017. A statistically significant difference was found between the PBS scores for the KT + SMO and barefoot (p = 0.012) interventions, and between the AFO and barefoot (p = 0.011) interventions. There was no significant difference between the AFO and KT + SMO interventions (p = 0.072) for the PBS, or between any of the interventions for the TUG. DISCUSSION: This case study explored the use of Kinesiotape® and SMOs as an alternative for children with spastic diplegic CP who require AFOs. Since KT + SMOs were statistically as effective as AFOs for improving balance and gait, as measured by the PBS and TUG, it was determined this is an effective alternative. For children who do not like to wear their AFOs, such as our participant, they may be more compliant in wearing SMOs and KT. Also, KT+SMOs does not limit ankle plantar flexion and dorsiflexion, which may allow for strengthening of the ankle muscles potentially resulting in improved push off and foot clearance during gait. Children can also work on balance reactions at the ankle when wearing KT and SMOs, which may assist with improving balance and decreasing falls. Lastly, for those children who do not like the appearance of AFOS they may be less self-conscious wearing KT and SMOs and find their peers more accepting. A HEALTH AND WELLNESS EDUCATION PROGRAM FOR ADULTS WITH DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES AT GOODWILL COLUMBUS Brock JM, Ellsworth D, Koski E, Leser K, Carey H and Nahikian-Nelms M. The Ohio State University Nisonger Center, Columbus, OH BACKGROUND & PURPOSE: Adults with developmental disabilities (DD) experience disparities in health conditions such as heart disease, obesity, and diabetes when compared to peers without DD. The amount of physical activity and the food choices these individuals make have a negative impact on these health conditions. Approximately 50% of adults with DD do not meet national physical activity recommendations. The majority of adults with DD living in community settings do not consume the recommended number of fruits and vegetables each week. The purpose of this project was to promote the health and wellness of adults with DD by increasing healthy lifestyle choices pertaining to physical activity and nutrition through the implementation of a modified version of the published “Health Matters” program. CASE DESCRIPTION: Sixteen adults with DD attending the SAGE program at Goodwill Columbus participated in an 8-week educational curriculum. They attended eight, one-hour health education classes covering nutrition and physical activity topics. They were encouraged to participate in structured physical activity programs at Goodwill as well as engage in similar activities at home. Program outcome data collected included: weight, BMI, waist circumference, heart rate, blood pressure, timed sit-to-stand, timed single leg balance, and information about lunch packing food choices. OUTCOMES: There were no significant changes on outcome measures found when comparing intervention and control groups at both pretest and posttest, however, there was a trend for changes in the intervention group. Intervention group participants lost an average of 4.5 pounds, 0.36 BMI points, and 1-inch off of their waists between pretest and posttest measurements. No changes were measured in foods consumed at lunch over the 8 weeks and only 2 participants consistently met MyPlate recommendations. Although measurable changes were minimal, by the end of the program, 100% of intervention participants reported “loving” or “liking” being physically active and eating fruits and vegetables. DISCUSSION: Although there were no statistically significant differences on the outcome measures as a result of the program much was learned about implementing health and wellness programming for adults with DD in a community setting.
