records.title: Flow as a positive affective state with optimal activation: converging physiological and self-report evidence in video games
records.abstract: Engaging experiences often occur when we are deeply absorbed in a challenging activity matching our skills-a state known as flow. Widely sought after in education, sports, and gaming, flow combines deep concentration with intrinsic enjoyment. Yet, its relationship with affective states remains debated. This study examined the relationship between flow and affect in video game players. Participants played a Tetris-like game under three difficulty conditions: too easy, optimal, and too difficult. Flow and affect were assessed through questionnaires, facial expressions, and physiological data (pupillometry, electrodermal activity, cardiac measures). The optimal condition was associated with the highest reported flow levels, increased positive affect, and moderate arousal. The too difficult condition triggered high arousal and negative affect, while the too easy condition showed low arousal. These results suggest that flow-related experiences may be associated with positive affective states, with implications for adaptive game design and player engagement monitoring.

records.title: Flow as Minimum-Displacement Maximum-Performance: Csikszentmihalyi's Optimal Experience as S⁰ Condition, Skill-Challenge Balance as Basin Geometry, and the Neurochemistry of Return
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: We apply the Displacement Framework to flow states (optimal experience), formalizing flow as the S0 condition for skilled performance: the state from which task execution costs the least. The skill-challenge balance is reinterpreted as basin geometry — boredom and anxiety are wrong attractors on either side of the flow channel, where challenge-to-skill ratio deviates from unity. We derive five propositions covering boredom as understimulation wrong attractor, anxiety as HPA activation wrong attractor, skill growth as basin migration, transient hypofrontality as monitoring-displacement reduction, and intrinsic reward as return signal. The neurochemistry of flow (dopamine, norepinephrine, anandamide, endorphins) is mapped to DF interpretations. Applications to education (ZPD as flow channel), sport psychology, creative work, musical improvisation, and meditation are developed. Wrong attractors that block flow (perfectionism, distraction, fear of failure) are formalized.

records.title: Flow Experience in Extensive Reading: Indonesian EFL Students’ Perceptions and Enabling Conditions
records.venue: Voices of English Language Education Society
records.abstract: Flow experience (FE) refers to an optimal psychological state characterized by deep involvement, enjoyment, and a sense of control during an activity. Although extensive reading (ER) is widely recognized for supporting language development, less is known about the psychological conditions that sustain learners’ engagement in ER, particularly in Indonesian EFL contexts. This study investigated Indonesian EFL students’ perceptions of FE during a two-semester ER program and examined the internal and external conditions that enabled or hindered flow. Thirty-six undergraduate English Literature students at a private university in West Java participated in the study while completing ER using the XReading platform across two consecutive semesters. A mixed-methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected at the end of each semester using a 36-item Flow State Scale covering nine dimensions of flow. Qualitative data were then gathered through semi-structured interviews with six purposively selected students representing diverse ER achievement patterns, complemented by document analysis of XReading logs and ER-related written tasks. Results indicated that students generally experienced high levels of flow in both semesters, with higher overall flow reported in the second semester. The largest increase was observed in skill–challenge balance, suggesting that sustained ER participation strengthened learners’ ability to select texts that matched their developing proficiency. Across both semesters, book content emerged as the most influential external condition, while mood and concentration were the most salient internal conditions. Interview findings further highlighted learner autonomy in selecting texts and managing reading routines as central to students’ sense of control and immersion, although competing academic and personal demands could disrupt flow. The findings suggest that two-semester ER programs can foster sustained flow when learners have access to engaging, level-appropriate texts and meaningful autonomy, supported by teacher guidance to help students regulate attention and affect.

records.title: Flow in Everyday Life: Activity Domains, Individual Differences, and Wellbeing Outcomes
records.abstract: The purpose of this study is to provide a comprehensive examination of how individuals experience flow in everyday life and how these experiences translate into wellbeing, using four complementary analytic approaches applied to the same two-wave dataset. In doing so, we explicitly distinguish between where flow is most likely to occur in daily life and where it is most consequential for wellbeing. First, consistent with flow theory, we test whether individuals experience different levels of flow across physical, academic, and maintenance activities (domains that vary naturally in challenge–skill balance, clarity of goals, and environmental structure) and assess which domain-specific flow experiences are most strongly associated with wellbeing. Second, we evaluate a conditional process model in which strengths use and playfulness facilitate flow, flow proneness strengthens these effects as a dispositional capacity for entering flow, and vitality functions as a state-based energetic resource that determines how strongly flow promotes wellbeing. Third, we examine individual differences by testing whether baseline personality, self-regulation, and flow proneness predict changes in flow and wellbeing over time, and whether vitality moderates the degree to which flow contributes to wellbeing gains. Finally, we investigate activity-specific goal engagement as a pathway into flow, testing whether individuals who engage more deeply with their goals experience more flow within each domain, and whether vitality moderates the conversion of goal engagement into flow. Collectively, these analyses offer an integrated account of how personal strengths, playful engagement, trait capacities, energetic resources, and goal-directed behaviour shape flow and wellbeing in everyday life.

records.title: Flow State in Live Music Performance: A Qualitative Study on Musicians’ Stage Experiences
records.abstract: This exploratory qualitative study examines how 32 professional musicians in Turkey described flow during live performance, and the conditions they perceived as facilitating or constraining it. Using a qualitative descriptive design with a phenomenological orientation and maximum-variation sampling, we conducted semi-structured interviews immediately after live sets to obtain performance-proximal accounts rather than implementing real-time experience sampling method (ESM) prompts. Reflexive thematic analysis of the interviews generated five themes: (1) definitions of flow (intense focus, altered time perception, unity with the music, present-centredness, well-being), (2) moments when flow tended to arise (improvisation, emotional or high-energy passages, stage entry), (3) external conditions (audience interaction, group energy, sound/technical reliability, unexpected events), (4) internal conditions (genre affinity, challenge–skill fit, music-theoretical orientation), and (5) perceived effects on performance (technical fluency, automaticity, effortlessness, expressiveness, creativity). Participants’ accounts highlight how flow in Turkish live-music venues is shaped by situated interactions with audiences, ensembles, and stage infrastructures, including genre-specific technical demands (e.g., bağlama performance). Overall, the study provides context-bound, experience-near insight into on-stage flow in contemporary Turkish popular music settings.

records.title: Flow State While Using Mixed Reality to Create Episodic Digital Experiences
records.abstract: This study investigates the intersection of flow states and Mixed Reality (MR) technology within artistic creation and immersive storytelling, emphasizing the transformative potential of MR tools in enhancing creativity, collaboration, and engagement. By integrating MR into artistic workflows, the research highlights how adaptability and perseverance in navigating advanced technologies can drive innovative practices, offering valuable insights for artists, designers, and technologists. The primary objective of this research is to explore how MR art authoring tools can facilitate flow states in creative processes and enable the creation of episodic extended reality (XR) experiences that seamlessly merge digital and physical realities. A qualitative methodology was employed, centered on collaborative artistic experiments conducted during an artist residency at Silpakorn University's Faculty of Decorative Arts. Participants included an experienced XR artist, Master’s and Ph.D. student, and faculty members. Workshops, seminars, and real-world applications of MR tools—such as Gravity Sketch, Open Brush, Nomad Sculpt, and Adobe Aero—provided a platform to analyze the dynamics of flow states in MR environments. The findings reveal that MR tools effectively induce flow states, characterized by time distortion, fulfillment, and autotelic behavior. Episodic XR storytelling emerged as a compelling medium for immersive artistic expression, with characters like Jaffa the biscuit maker and Juju the little pig exemplifying the imaginative possibilities of MR technology. Participants demonstrated heightened engagement, collaboration, and adaptability, overcoming technological challenges while reimagining physical spaces through geospatially anchored augmented reality (AR) experiences. The study underscores the importance of maintaining a flexible and experimental mindset to navigate the complexities of emerging technologies. It highlights the synergistic relationship between flow psychology and MR tools, emphasizing the critical role of play in unlocking creativity and fostering genuine self-expression. The collaborative and iterative processes observed affirm MR's potential to inspire dynamic narratives, transform artistic workflows, and contribute to the evolving understanding of flow states and digital creativity in contemporary art practice of storytelling that emphasizes the impact that technology has on the production of immersive media.

records.title: Flow-Related Engagement in Children Undergoing Cancer Treatment in China: A Scoping Review of Psychosocial and Digital Interventions
records.abstract: This scoping review aims to map and synthesize existing evidence regarding flow-related engagement among children undergoing cancer treatment in China, with a particular focus on psychosocial and digital interventions. Flow theory describes an optimal psychological state characterized by deep concentration, intrinsic motivation, perceived control, enjoyment, and balance between challenge and skill. Although flow has been extensively studied in educational, occupational, and digital contexts, its application in pediatric oncology remains limited. Existing interventions used in pediatric oncology, including therapeutic play, expressive arts, medical play, shared reading, virtual reality, and digital gaming, frequently incorporate elements associated with flow-related engagement; however, these mechanisms have not been systematically mapped. This scoping review will identify and characterise psychosocial and digital interventions that promote engagement-related experiences among children undergoing cancer treatment in Chinese contexts. The review will examine how flow-related constructs are conceptualised, operationalised, and represented within existing interventions and will identify gaps requiring future research.

records.title: FOREIGN EXPERIENCE IN DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION OF STATE-OWNED ROAD INFRASTRUCTURE ENTERPRISES
records.abstract:
Objective: To identify replicable digital transformation practices for state-owned road infrastructure enterprises that reduce operating costs, improve the reliability of road assets, increase road network capacity, and improve the quality of services provided.
Objectives: To systematize international experience in applying advanced digital technologies in state-owned road infrastructure enterprises; to identify the main barriers to implementing digital technologies in state-owned road infrastructure enterprises and to analyze effective mechanisms for overcoming them based on international experience; to identify key factors for the success of digital transformation, taking into account the specifics of the public road infrastructure sector; and to develop practical recommendations for the systemic integration of technological, organizational, and management components to ensure reproducible and sustainable results in the digitalization of road infrastructure.
Methodology. To identify replicable digital transformation practices for state-owned road infrastructure enterprises, a comparative case study of international experience in implementing digital technologies in the road sector was conducted for the period 2020–2025.
Results. Standard architectures of digital solutions for state-owned road infrastructure enterprises have been systematized. It has been established that effective digital transformation of the road sector relies on a specific technological architecture, including automatic weigh-in systems that continuously monitor traffic flows and prevent premature roadway wear; an audit of infrastructure readiness for autonomous vehicle operation, assessing the quality of markings and signs for driver assistance systems; virtual models of road infrastructure with the integration of asset lifecycle data; and systems for cooperative interaction between vehicles and infrastructure based on wireless communication technologies. Critical factors for the success of digital transformation of the road sector have been identified: ensuring intersystem interaction through open software interfaces and industry data standards, standardizing road asset telemetry, developing digital competencies of personnel, and overcoming data fragmentation through the formation of a unified digital ecosystem. It has been established that sustainable and reproducible results are achieved through a comprehensive approach that overcomes key barriers—such as a lack of competencies and data fragmentation—by developing an integrated digital road infrastructure ecosystem.
Conclusions. Effective digital transformation of state-owned road infrastructure enterprises is based on the systemic integration of technological, organizational, and management components. Sustainable results are achieved through a comprehensive approach that overcomes key barriers by creating an integrated digital ecosystem. The specific nature of the public sector requires consideration of specific corporate governance models and protection of state interests when implementing digital initiatives. The identified replicable practices and standard architectures can be adapted to various organizational structures for road infrastructure management.

records.title: Formation of a conceptual model and principles for building a digital ecosystem for the sustainable development of specially protected natural areas
records.abstract:
Aim.
  To develop a conceptual architecture and scientifically grounded principles for the functioning of a digital ecosystem aimed at ensuring a balance between recreational activity, the investment attractiveness of specially protected natural areas (SPNAs), and biodiversity conservation objectives within the framework of the national ESG agenda.
 
 
 Objectives.
  To conduct a critical analysis of the current state of digitalization in managing tourist flows within SPNAs of the Russian Federation; to identify the economic barriers to crossindustry collaboration between businesses and conservation institutions; to substantiate the need to transition from static recreational capacity standards to dynamic models based on big data; to develop the component structure of a digital solution that integrates geoanalytics, ecosystem services economics, and distributed ledger tools.
 
 
 Methods.
  The research is based on the methodology of enterprise architecture systems analysis, the platform economy concept, and agent-based simulation methods (AnyLogic). The empirical foundation includes reported data on visitor numbers from pilot national parks and the results of an analysis of existing geographic information system (GIS) solutions used by the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment of the Russian Federation.
 
 
 Results.
  The study presents the author’s conceptual model of a three-level digital ecosystem for SPNAs (data collection verification monetization of ecosystem services). The analysis reveals that the key driver for implementing platform solutions is industrial partners’ need for verifiable carbon footprint reduction and biodiversity offset units. The study demonstrates the economic efficiency of dynamic anthropogenic load regulation compared to traditional administrative restrictions. The paper proposes principles for integrating a digital twin of a tourist destination with corporate ESG reporting systems.
 
 
 Conclusions.
  The developed model enables the transformation of SPNAs from subsidized entities into active participants in the green financial instruments market, thereby creating a sustainable economic foundation for preserving natural heritage. Practical application of the model is constrained by the absence of an industry standard for geospatial data exchange and insufficient legal certainty regarding the status of ecosystem services in Russian legislation.

records.title: FORMATION OF A MECHANISM FOR NEUTRALIZING BUSINESS ACTIVITY RISKS OF AGRIBUSINESS ENTERPRISES
records.abstract: The article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations for the formation and functioning of a mechanism for neutralizing business activity risks of agribusiness enterprises under conditions of increasing uncertainty in the external environment. It is substantiated that agribusiness is one of the most risk-prone sectors of the economy due to its dependence on natural and climatic conditions, fluctuations in agricultural product prices, logistical constraints, wartime threats, and instability of state policy. In this context, an effective risk neutralization system is considered an essential component of the overall enterprise management mechanism and a prerequisite for ensuring financial stability and competitiveness. The economic essence of the concept of a “mechanism for neutralizing business activity risks” is revealed, its place within the management system of an agricultural enterprise is determined, and the main functions, principles, and tools for its implementation are characterized. Scientific approaches of domestic and foreign scholars to the classification of agribusiness risks – particularly production, financial, market, institutional, and environmental risks – are generalized, which made it possible to develop a comprehensive approach to their identification and assessment. The study analyzes contemporary scientific publications from 2021 to 2025, which emphasize riskoriented management, digital tools for risk monitoring, agricultural risk insurance, diversification of production and financial flows, and other modern approaches. Special attention is paid to the impact of military actions, climate change, and global crises on the level of agribusiness risks, which necessitates the formation of flexible, adaptive, and preventive mechanisms for their neutralization. Key problems of risk management in agribusiness enterprises are identified, including the fragmented nature of risk management, limited use of modern analytical tools, insufficient insurance coverage, and a low level of integration of risk management into the strategic planning system. The expediency of improving the risk neutralization mechanism is substantiated through the combination of financial, organizational, technological, and information instruments, the development of internal control systems, and the implementation of digital risk management platforms. It is concluded that an effectively formed mechanism for neutralizing business activity risks enhances the adaptability of agribusiness enterprises to changes in the external environment, reduces losses, and ensures sustainable development in the long term. The research results can be applied in the management practice of agricultural enterprises and in further scientific studies on risk management in agribusiness.

records.title: FORMATION OF THE DIGITAL TRADE MODEL: INTERNATIONAL TRENDS
records.abstract:
Annotation. The presented article investigates the formation and evolution of digital trade models within the framework of contemporary global economic transformations. The research focuses on the structural components of digital trade, including the development of electronic commerce platforms, the integration of fintech solutions, the digitalization of logistics and supply chain systems, and the modernization of customs and border procedures through digital technologies. A comparative analysis of international experience is conducted by examining the digital trade practices of China, South Korea, Germany, the United Kingdom, Turkey, the United States, Japan, and Georgia. The paper identifies the key strengths and limitations of each national model and evaluates their relevance for emerging digital economies. Based on these findings, the study outlines strategic directions and policy recommendations for the effective adaptation and implementation of a digital trade model in Azerbaijan.

Key words: Digital trade model, international digital trade, e-commerce platforms, fintech integration, digital logistics, smart customs systems, digital transformation, global trade trends, cross-border e-commerce, digital economy, etc.

Introduction

In the contemporary era, digitalization has emerged as one of the primary drivers of global economic development, profoundly influencing international trade systems. The rapid advancement of information and communication technologies, the widespread adoption of electronic commerce platforms, and the integration of financial technologies (fintech) into trade operations have transformed traditional trade mechanisms, leading to the emergence of a comprehensive digital trade model. This model encompasses not only the online sale of goods and services but also the digital management of logistics, customs administration, payment systems, and supply chains.

The level of digital trade development has become a critical indicator of national economic competitiveness. In this context, the experiences of countries such as China, South Korea, Germany, the United Kingdom, Turkey, the United States, Japan, and Georgia provide valuable insights. These countries implement diverse models of digital trade, combining government policies, innovative technological applications, and the integration of business entities into digital commerce. Examining these experiences, analyzing their strengths and weaknesses, and assessing their applicability is crucial for formulating an optimal digital trade model for Azerbaijan.

The objective of this article is to systematically analyze the global trends in digital trade model formation and to identify strategic directions for enhancing Azerbaijan’s digital trade potential. The study explores both theoretical approaches and international best practices, evaluating the structural components of digital trade and their potential adaptation to the Azerbaijani economic context.

The Concept of Digital Trade

Digital trade has emerged as a central phenomenon in the development of the global economy, reflecting the transformation of traditional trade mechanisms. Unlike conventional trade, which is often constrained by geographical and physical limitations, digital trade accelerates cross-border transactions, reduces operational costs, and optimizes interactions between market participants. Digital trade encompasses not only the online sale of goods and services but also a complex set of components, including fintech systems, digital logistics, electronic platforms, and smart customs solutions, which collectively enhance the efficiency, transparency, and competitiveness of global commerce.

E-commerce: E-commerce refers to the sale and management of goods and services through digital platforms. This process extends beyond mere transactions, integrating payment processing, order tracking, and logistics coordination. International platforms such as Alibaba, Amazon, eBay, and Shopify serve as prominent examples, facilitating both retail and cross-border operations. By combining payment solutions and logistics services, these platforms significantly improve operational efficiency and market transparency.

Digital platforms: Digital platforms are complex systems that connect buyers and sellers within a virtual marketplace. They enable participants to engage in global commerce, increase market transparency, and simplify the management of trade operations. Furthermore, these platforms provide advanced analytical capabilities, allowing businesses to assess consumer behavior, optimize pricing strategies, and enhance overall market competitiveness.

Digital logistics and supply chain management: Digital logistics involves monitoring goods and services throughout the supply chain, managing inventories, optimizing delivery processes, and digitalizing customs operations. These systems ensure optimal inventory levels, reduce delivery costs, and enable rapid responses to customer demands. Smart customs and digital document flows further enhance cross-border trade efficiency while minimizing compliance risks.

Fintech: Fintech constitutes a core component of digital trade, encompassing innovative financial technologies such as electronic payment systems, digital wallets, blockchain technologies, and smart contracts. By increasing the speed, security, and transparency of transactions, fintech solutions play a crucial role in facilitating international payments and streamlining export operations.

The expansion of digital trade creates new opportunities for both public and private sectors. Governments promote trade activities through the development of digital infrastructure, enhancement of legal frameworks, and implementation of smart customs systems, while private enterprises lead in platform management, innovative fintech applications, and optimization of digital logistics. Consequently, digital trade not only accelerates economic growth but also contributes significantly to the transparency, efficiency, and sustainability of global trade processes.

Digital Trade Models

The development of digital trade varies across countries, depending on different strategies and governance approaches. Generally, these approaches can be grouped into three main models: state-driven, market-driven, and hybrid models. Each model is shaped by a country\\\`s economic structure, digital infrastructure, and government policies, contributing uniquely to the advancement of digital trade.

China and South Korea are typical examples of countries following the state-driven model in digital trade. In these nations, the government plays a central role in establishing the digital ecosystem, facilitating rapid development of digital platforms through strategic planning, investment support, and regulatory initiatives. In China, under government leadership, large e-commerce platforms have been developed, alongside digital payment systems and smart customs solutions, significantly enhancing both export and domestic trade efficiency. In South Korea, digital trade has expanded rapidly, particularly due to technological infrastructure development and government-supported startup programs.

This growth is reflected in concrete digital trade indicators. For instance, in South Korea, the proportion of businesses placing orders (i.e., making purchases) over computer networks was 48.27% in 2010, rising to 59.68% in 2011. It reached 61.95% in 2012, then slightly declined to 59.26% in 2013. In 2014, the indicator dropped to 50.70%, reaching a minimum of 34.44% in 2015. records.title: Formative assessment and emotional trajectories aiding investigation of flow in higher education
records.abstract: Introduction Flow represents a psychologically optimal state characterized by deep engagement, intrinsic motivation, and a balance between perceived challenge and skill. While formative assessment is known to support self-regulated learning through feedback and reflection, its relationship with students' emotional trajectories toward flow in higher education remains insufficiently explored. This study investigates how formative assessment practices are associated with the development of emotional states consistent with progression toward flow in university mathematics courses. Methods The study was conducted over three academic years (2020-2022) with 70 undergraduate students enrolled in mathematics-related courses. A design-based research approach was implemented in a feedback-rich instructional environment combining project-based learning, weekly formative feedback cycles, co-assessment activities, and a two-day hackathon. Students reported their emotional states weekly using a structured self-report instrument based on Csikszentmihalyi's eight-state model. Longitudinal changes were analysed using cumulative link mixed models and transition-probability analyses. Results Students' emotional states showed a significant upward progression over time, with the average category increasing from 4.19 in week 1 to 7.31 in week 12. Negative emotional states such as worry and anxiety were more frequent at the beginning of the course, whereas activating states (arousal and flow) peaked during the intermediate phase, with flow reported by 60% of students in week 10. Control and relaxation increased steadily toward the end of the semester, reaching 86% combined in the final week. Statistical modelling confirmed a strong positive effect of time on transitions toward higher emotional-state categories. Discussion The findings indicate that sustained formative assessment practices were associated with emotionally productive learning trajectories consistent with progression toward flow. Weekly feedback cycles and collaborative learning activities appeared to support gradual shifts from uncertainty to engagement and finally to confidence and stability. These results suggest that formative assessment can function as a pedagogical mechanism for fostering optimal learning experiences in higher education mathematics contexts.

records.title: Fostering a culture of inquiry through a dedicated Nursing Research Clinic: a mixed-methods evaluation of the CREATE model
records.abstract: Background: Despite widespread recognition of evidence-based practice as fundamental to quality healthcare, persistent theory-to-practice gaps undermine optimal patient outcomes. Structural barriers including inadequate mentorship, limited resources, and organizational constraints prevent clinical nurses from engaging meaningfully in research activities. Objective: To evaluate the observed changes in clinical nurses' research competencies and inquiry cultures associated with a novel Nursing Research Clinic operationalized through the CREATE (Consultation, Review, Enlighten, Advice, Ticket, Enhancement) model. Design: Convergent parallel mixed-methods design employing a single-group pre-post intervention assessment with qualitative exploration of participant experiences. Methods: Following institutional ethics approval, 86 registered nurses with ≥1-year clinical experience participated in the CREATE intervention at Beijing Tsinghua Changgeng Hospital (October 2023-October 2024). Perceived research competence was assessed pre- and post-intervention using the Nursing Research Competence Self-Assessment Scale (NRCSAS), a 30-item instrument adapted for clinical nurses from a previously published research competency scale. Research productivity metrics were tracked, and semi-structured interviews with 20 participants explored experiences through inductive thematic analysis. Results: = 1.09). Early-stage productivity outcomes included one core journal publication, three national presentations, three patents, and four funded projects. Qualitative analysis revealed five themes: transformation from apprehension to empowerment, catalytic mentorship role, legitimization through institutional recognition, enhanced collaboration, and navigation of research challenges. Conclusion: The CREATE model represents a structured and replicable intervention that systematically addresses barriers to nursing research engagement. This evaluation demonstrates that the model is associated with meaningful improvements in research competence and early-stage scholarly productivity, supported by qualitative evidence of professional identity transformation, mentorship effectiveness, and institutional legitimization. Future multi-site-controlled studies are recommended to further establish generalizability and long-term sustainability.

records.title: Four Frameworks for Viewing Blended Learning Cases
records.abstract: The five studies of blended learning implementations in this issue share a certain verve and enthusiasm. The time is right for this “old friend with a new name,” blended learning. It is enjoyable to read these studies, and share in the hope and the enthusiasm generated by the positive comments of students and instructors who have been affected. This enthusiasm and wide political support is breaking down the cultural divide between systematic and research-based instructional design and conventional teaching pointed out by Rose (2003). The teaching culture and the systematic designers have long lived in different worlds and have not had as much impact on one another as would be hoped. We see an accommodation happening in these studies, even as we see the main divisive element, efficiency and lower costs through technology, surfacing as overt goals in these studies. Part of this is due to the BYU environment, but an important part as well may be that the faculty role is blended, expanded and changed, but not threatened.My comments are organized around four conceptual frameworks. All four are coming from the science or engineering-based culture of design, research, and continuing evaluation that is being embraced, at least gingerly, by the teachers, administrators, and designers in these studies. The four frameworks are:Called “case studies” in these articles, and even given the lowly name “pilots” by Christensen, each of the studies evidences being set in a sequence of implementations, followed by design of improvements, followed by successive implementations. The most self-aware of these iterative cycles was Christensen's study. She approaches a disciplined comparison of the newly-designed blended study with its predecessor version of the classroom-taught instructional design course. In what is reported as the first cycle, she and her co-teacher document the design changes they made to make the course a blended learning experience consistent with constructivist pedagogy. When a design study appeals to models or theory, even a model rough as the constructivist principles, we would call the design study “principled.” Her designs as reported are clear and principled, though obviously informed much by the craft lore, artfully applied, of the discipline of instructional design methods she teaches. She also reports the design changes made after the first cycle, and the improved results obtained. She concludes with a clear statement consistent with the logic of design studies: “The challenge, then, is to fine-tune the strategies through successive iterations …” Her iterations of design and evaluation deal with such issues as finding the right balance between web and group activities, reducing negative consequences, and improving effectiveness.One danger of not crediting the power of the J-curve is apparent in her article. Due to negative feedback and marginal value of the first attempt at online peer review, this was abandoned and replaced with face-to-face discussions in class. Yet a key problem in this and other studies like it is that “responding to individual students required a serious investment of my time.” It is known that peer review can be implemented well, can get good results, and can reduce the teacher's grading and feedback time. As a related example, the teacher in the third study had, with experience, cut back on his time in responding to posted messages, relying increasingly on getting the dialogue going well, then only stepping in occasionally. Recognizing that some interventions change habits and practices too much all at once, and that the implementation plan needs to be adjusted to prevent difficulties the next time, perhaps the peer review in Case 1 could have been rehabilitated, rather than pushing it all back on the instructor.Except possibly for Case 2, all of the cases could have explained themselves better, and made more useful comparisons, by placing themselves in a framework of a sequence of design studies, and recognizing the J-curve effect. Case 5 is an exciting beginning that could become a series of design studies. Like Case 1, it reported on two semesters of implementation (but only the designed changes in semester 2, not the results). Case 5 is incredibly ambitious, redesigning writing courses taken by 30,000 students and using hundreds of graduate instructors. It was the best funded study of the group, with both substantial university and Pew Foundation funds, and with formal evaluation funded specifically, rather than as an “out-of-hide” expectation on the faculty or as a low-budget student project. Interpreted as a J-curve, it is a positive, not a problem that such a small, non-statistically significant dip was experienced the first time in comparison with traditional classes. There was also small evidence of student writing improvement on two aspects of the scoring rubric.It is good news, not bad, that the instructors were not well motivated nor involved, because introducing features such as the ones they have already proposed for the second semester, it may be possible to get the buy-in and commitment missing the first cycle from the instructors, taking the slope of the J up each semester as improvements are made. Perhaps I detected a note of defensiveness in the discussion of all the changes made to correct problems revealed by the evaluation. This would be normal, after such a large expenditure of leadership and financial capital had produced nothing spectacular.If a bit of commonly-experienced defensiveness does exist, a forthright grounding of the work as a sequence of design studies (design experiments if the outcome measures become more comparable and valid, and the design changes more principled), takes away any defensiveness. It would then be understood from the first that new implementations, especially with a large group of instructors, are likely to produce no improvement – even a dip from baseline the first cycle, but that the instructional system is now in a form that can be rapidly improved and revised (one of the benefits listed by Osguthorpe and Graham). The greatest improvements related to the J, however, are likely to come as a result of adaptations in the implementation plan – roles (new training and job-aids), rules (new course procedures) and not just in the tools (learning objects, on-line assignment handling, and the like).Case 5 could also have been improved, had it been conceived from the first as a design study or design experiment. More time and resources would have been expended documenting the baseline – the results and features of the English 115 experience before the change. This is true of every one of the five studies. Some mention was always made of what had happened before the study, but it was clear that some of the cases were well along in a series of implementations and try-outs, followed by design changes, while others (e.g., studies 2 and 5) were more truly the first cycle. The addition of the web-based features that justify the designation “blended learning” is only the latest change by some of these innovative and adventurous teachers. It is clear that this is the case in studies one, three, four. In a sequence of design studies, some of these teachers had already removed some of the glitches and mistakes of first-timers and had developed more seasoned habits. Looking backward and documenting some of these learnings is important in writing up such studies. Take a longer view. What is the baseline? Which semester is really cycle 1? How many semesters can we keep the improvement-oriented sequence going, and how far up the J can we move? What metrics (usually more than one) can we use to make the plotting of the J more rigorous, and comparisons between cycles more attributable to introduced design changes?Some of the most exciting and promising results in this suite of blended learning studies come from student comments about the great benefit they received from increased dialogue with fellow students. Consider Case 3, a snap-shot partway up the J-curve for an adaptive, innovative instructor. This instructor had used on-line discussion boards before, and “He found individual responses [to student posts] to be especially important during the first month of the semester, when distance learners were becoming familiar with the technology.” In the ECD framework, the first moderating functions are designed to help students “survive” the initial onslaught of technical issues unrelated to the course content, then right after that, to establish a “feeling of belonging” These early moderating functions help students to overcome the fear of rejection or being ignored or laughed at. Once these levels are achieved, a collaborative discourse can accelerate, and can increasingly focus on the content.Moderating functions are needed to keep the group on track, and to keep the give and take going. This give and take can be very motivating. Later moderating functions, such as “weaving”—putting together comments of others, with excerpts from readings, into a higher synthesis helpful to everyone—can lead to high levels of real intellectual engagement. This is exhilarating for the teacher, and for the students alike. In Case 3, “the instructor was able to see that this objective [learners becoming more conscientious scholars] was being met. He was especially pleased when learners would include links to articles or include valuable references he had not previously accessed.” High-level synthesizing and weaving comments in student posts are a new form of evaluation data useful in detecting higher levels of intellectual engagement.An understanding of the the use of and response to moderating functions by instructors and students alike in the use and response to moderating functions can inform implementations of cases other than Case 3. In Case 2, teaching and applying an understanding of ECD and moderating functions could benefit the dynamics of the blended class significantly. It could benefit interactions locally and collaboration with the distance students. Encouragement through moderating functions would help all students feel more involved and would facilitate the effectiveness of the chat sessions as well. ECD through asynchrounous seminars could be added in a later cycle to further enhance collaborative discourse for all. Lessons from ECD apply in Case 4 as well. Here, the students engage in group discussions, with an overt goal to help them operate at higher levels of critical thinking—the upper end of the moderating function continuum—promoting intellectual engagement. Moderating functions can be applied in oral situations as well as in computer text dialogues. Also, in future cycles of implementation, the instructors in the accounting classes might consider the use of asynchronous computer conferences. If not feasible in the 100 student classes, perhaps in later, smaller classes where intellectual engagement is the clear goal.Case 5 offers some of the greatest benefits potential benefit attainable through teaching instructors to use computer conferences and peer reviews to teach the writing process. In cycle 1, instructors traded off office hours, direct instruction, and other matters for 110 minutes, on average, of email. If they knew the ECD process, and the high levels of intellectually engage application of writing principles attainable thereby, it might bode well for increasing their own intellectual engagement and feeling of accomplishment.A few comments reported from students interviewed or polled in these studies showed individuals reflecting the need for accommodation to their differences. In Case 4, one student said “I just wish that on some of the easy points, you could click through a little faster.” This is the kind of comment that would be made by a transforming learner, the most eager, self-confident, and autonomous of the four levels of the learning orientation construct. records.title: FRAGMENTED CROSS-BORDER DATA FLOWS REGULATIONS: IMPLICATIONS FOR DIGITISATION OF TRADE IN AFRICA
records.abstract: This dissertation examines Africa’s fragmented regulatory environment for cross-border data flows and the consequences of that fragmentation for continental digital integration. Using doctrinal analysis of key continental and regional instruments, data sovereignty as a conceptual tool, it argues that Africa’s regulatory landscape is fragmented across continental and regional layers which has birthed different discretionally expressions at the national level. Also, a comparative legal assessment of the EU’s GDPR and the AU’s data governance framework and through the lens of the Brussels Effect, the dissertation further argues that the GDPR’s extraterritorial influence has encouraged legal transplantation in many African jurisdictions, leading to the adoption of rules that appear internationally compliant but remain misaligned with the AU’s integration and sovereignty objectives. The findings show an apparent convergence across Africa around a conditional transfer mode, often expressed through adequacy-style requirements, yet this surface-level agreement obscures deeper fragmentation in legal form, institutional capability, and technological readiness. At the continental level, the Malabo Convention, the AU Data Policy Framework, and the AfCFTA digital instruments display persistent gaps between stated ambition and reality, this is reflected in low ratification or weak implementation pathways, conceptual indeterminacy, and limited institutional support. This disintegration is replicated at the Regional Economic Communities. The study also argues that the quest for data sovereignty is a legitimate claim for most African states, but its fragmented expression weakens the collective voice of the AU and in turn, its digital trade ambitions. The dissertation concludes that Africa’s digital transformation agenda requires a model that combines baseline binding continental standards with flexible implementation, supported by stronger coordinating institutions, capacity-building, and infrastructural development, while preserving interoperability for global digital trade.

records.title: From  AIE-Pharmacology to Fluoropharmacology: The Paradigm Evolution of Disciplinary Framework  Based on the "Drug-Probe Unity" Concept
records.abstract: From AIE-Pharmacology to Fluoropharmacology: The Paradigm Evolution of Disciplinary Framework Based on the "Drug-Probe Unity" ConceptXinghua YuDepartment of Urology & Andrology, Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, 310016, China.E-mail: yuxinghua@zju.edu.cn AbstractAIE-pharmacology, as a deep integration of traditional pharmacology and aggregation-induced emission technology, has proposed a theoretical framework of "multi-level theranostics." Building upon this foundation, this paper further elaborates and proposes the disciplinary evolution from AIE-pharmacology to fluoropharmacology, with "Drug-Probe Unity" (DPU) as the core philosophical concept, encompassing a triple unity across ontology, epistemology, and praxis: Pharmacophore-Fluorophore Unity (PFU), Drug-Probe Unity (DPU), and Drug-Praxis Unity (DPU 2.0). Importantly, we establish a comprehensive classification of drug luminescent states upon aggregation—Aggregation-Caused Quenching (ACQ, 1-0), Aggregation-Induced Emission (AIE, 0-1), Aggregation-Retained Emission (ARE, 1-1), and Aggregation-Retained Non-emission (ARN, 0-0)—which provides the foundational framework for understanding the photophysical behavior of intrinsically luminescent drugs. This theoretical system not only transforms drug action from a "temporal black box" to a "spatiotemporal color map," but more importantly achieves a paradigm shift from "interpreting drugs" to "transforming therapy." The establishment of fluoropharmacology provides new methodological guidance for the precision development and clinical translation of small molecule drugs (accounting for approximately 90% of globally marketed drugs). Keywords: AIE-pharmacology; Fluoropharmacology; Drug-Probe Unity; theranostics; multi-level visualization; aggregation-induced emission; aggregation-retained emission 1 Introduction: From Luminescence Phenomena to Paradigmatic Reflection on PharmacologyThe original meaning of philosophy is "love of wisdom," and the Latin etymology of PhD (Philosophiae Doctor) is literally "Doctor of Philosophy"—this implies that any discipline, when traced to its foundations, will encounter systematic reflection on fundamental questions. Socrates' maxim "Know thyself" is not only an admonition for humans but can also be regarded as a metaphor for drug cognition: Do we truly know the entire journey of drugs within living organisms?Traditional pharmacology has long faced a fundamental dilemma: after drugs enter organisms, their action process resembles a "black box." We can observe inputs (administration) and outputs (efficacy and toxicity), but the spatiotemporal dynamic processes in between can only be inferred indirectly[1]. This cognitive limitation is analogous to the prolonged debate in philosophical history between materialism and idealism—can we transcend phenomena to grasp essence?Chinese philosophy provides unique intellectual resources for breaking through this dilemma. "Man-Nature Unity" emphasizes the organic wholeness of humans and nature, while "Knowledge-Action Unity" advocates the inseparability of understanding and practice. Inspired by these, we proposed the concept of "Drug-Probe Unity" (DPU) in AIE-pharmacology research: the drug molecule serves both as a therapeutic entity and an imaging probe—no longer two functionally separate modules externally combined, but an internally unified whole. The proposition of this concept marks a significant leap in drug epistemology[2, 3].Marx pointed out in his Theses on Feuerbach: "The philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways; the point is to change it." This thought provides profound methodological guidance—we should not only "interpret" why drugs luminesce, but use luminescence to "change" the practical dilemmas of clinical treatment. The evolution from AIE-pharmacology to fluoropharmacology is precisely the concrete practice of this philosophical turn in pharmaceutical research[4, 5].2 From ACQ to AIE: The Fluorescence Paradigm Shift and Its Pharmacological SignificanceConventional organic fluorescent dyes generally exhibit the aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ) phenomenon, a characteristic that severely limits their application in complex biological systems[6, 7]. When fluorescent molecules enter organisms, they inevitably accumulate at target regions, yet ACQ molecules paradoxically experience fluorescence attenuation or even extinction precisely in the aggregated state, creating a scenario where "the more they need to be observed, the less visible they become."The discovery of the aggregation-induced emission (AIE) phenomenon fundamentally changed this situation[8]. AIE molecules exhibit weak luminescence in dispersed states but significantly enhanced fluorescence upon aggregation[9]. This unique "anti-ACQ" characteristic makes them naturally suitable for target enrichment scenarios in vivo—the more precisely drugs reach their action sites and aggregate, the stronger their fluorescence signals become, and the clearer the observation[10-21]. This property of "more effective, more visible" provides unprecedented tools for pharmacological research.However, our systematic investigation of drug luminescent behavior upon aggregation has revealed that the AIE phenomenon, while revolutionary, represents only one of four possible photophysical outcomes[22-30]. We have established a comprehensive classification framework based on the binary states of molecular dispersion and aggregation:The Four Luminescent States of DrugsThis classification reveals that the relationship between aggregation state and luminescence is more nuanced than previously recognized. For fluoropharmacology, each state offers distinct advantages and limitations:ACQ (1-0) molecules, while traditional, face the fundamental limitation of signal loss precisely at the site of action where aggregation occurs—the "inverse correlation" problem.AIE (0-1) molecules provide the ideal "turn-on" sensing mechanism, with signal generation directly correlating with target engagement and accumulation. This makes them particularly valuable for real-time monitoring of drug distribution and target binding.ARE (1-1) molecules maintain constitutive fluorescence regardless of aggregation state. While this provides continuous visibility throughout the drug's journey, it may lack the signal-to-noise advantages of AIE's "turn-on" mechanism for distinguishing bound/free drug fractions.ARN (0-0) molecules, lacking luminescence entirely, fall outside the scope of fluoropharmacology unless modified to acquire fluorescent properties.For intrinsic AIE drugs—molecules that are both therapeutically active and possess AIE properties—the 0-1 binary code is fundamental: they exist in a non-emissive or weakly emissive state during circulation (0), and become brightly emissive upon reaching and aggregating at the target site (1). This "silent until action" property provides an ideal mechanism for distinguishing specifically bound drug from freely circulating drug, enabling precise spatiotemporal mapping of drug action.The discovery and characterization of AIE drugs, such as the natural product vitexin identified in our ferritin-nanocaged formulation for treating asthenospermia, exemplify this ideal 0-1 behavior. The 0-1 transition serves as an intrinsic reporter of target engagement, turning on precisely where and when therapeutic action occurs.AIE materials in biomedical applications have demonstrated significant advantages[31-44]. In antibacterial applications, AIE-active antibiotic photosensitizers possess five major advantages: broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, reduced antibiotic resistance, strong controllability, low toxicity, and high tissue selectivity[45-51]. In tumor theranostics, the development of ionic second near-infrared window AIE phototheranostic agents has enabled mitochondria-disruption-driven precision anti-tumor therapy, achieving precise tumor elimination guided by NIR-II fluorescence/photothermal imaging[52-57]. These advances indicate that AIE materials have evolved from simple imaging probes to "theranostic" platforms with integrated therapeutic functions[58, 59].However, most of the aforementioned research remains at the level of "applications of AIE materials in biomedicine," and has not yet ascended to systematic pharmacological theory. Genuine theoretical innovation requires elevating AIE from a "tool" to a "paradigm," from a "method" to a "discipline."3 The Theoretical Framework of AIE-Pharmacology: Multi-Level TheranosticsWe formally defined AIE drugs and AIE-pharmacology in Advanced Functional Materials (2025, e22020). AIE-pharmacology is the science studying the dynamic, bidirectional, and real-time visualizable interaction laws between drugs and organisms across all biological levels from molecules to systems. With "theranostics" as its core objective, it achieves spatiotemporal synchronization in analyzing drug in vivo journeys and mechanisms of action through intrinsically luminescent drugs or intelligent delivery systems.This theory extends traditional pharmacology into three interconnected and progressively deepening pillars:First Pillar: Systems Pharmacodynamics—How Drugs "Act" at Multiple Levels Drug effects are the ordered integration and emergence of specific events triggered at multiple biological levels. From molecular-level target binding, to organelle-level functional module responses, to cellular-level fate decisions, and finally to tissue-organ-system level physiological function outputs, the fluorescence signals of AIE drugs provide real-time observational evidence at each level. The 0-1 transition of AIE drugs enables precise identification of when and where each level of action occurs.Second Pillar: Dynamic Pharmacokinetics—How the Organism "Disposes" of Drugs at Multiple Levels The in vivo fate of a drug is a continuous process determined by every biological barrier it crosses and every layer of biotransformation it undergoes. AIE characteristics enable real-time visual mapping of the entire process of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion, particularly the dynamic processes of crossing special structures such as the blood-brain barrier and blood-testis barrier. The transition from non-emissive (0) to emissive (1) states marks critical junctures in this journey.Third Pillar: Theranostics—The Visual Bridge Connecting Pharmacodynamics and Pharmacokinetics By utilizing the drug's own AIE properties, the traditional "black box" process is transformed into a "visualized" process, enabling non-invasive real-time monitoring, immediate efficacy feedback, and intuitive mechanistic explanation.The establishment of this theoretical framework lays a solid foundation for the proposition of fluoropharmacology.4 The Proposition of Fluoropharmacology: From AIE Materials to AIE DrugsThe transition from AIE-pharmacology to fluoropharmacology represents a natural and necessary conceptual expansion. AIE-pharmacology, as initially proposed, focused specifically on drugs exhibiting aggregation-induced emission characteristics—the 0→1 transition that provides an ideal "turn-on" mechanism for reporting target engagement. This framework has proven revolutionary for understanding drug behavior through the lens of AIE phenomena.However, our systematic screening of existing drug libraries reveals a more complex reality: the majority of intrinsically luminescent small molecule drugs do not belong to the AIE category. Many clinically valuable drugs exhibit aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ, 1-0) behavior—they fluoresce in dispersed states but quench upon aggregation at target sites. Others demonstrate aggregation-retained emission (ARE, 1-1), maintaining constitutive fluorescence regardless of their aggregation state. All three categories—AIE (0-1), ACQ (1-0), and ARE (1-1)—represent intrinsically luminescent drugs that, by virtue of their inherent fluorescence, embody the core "Drug-Probe Unity" (DPU) concept.This recognition necessitates a paradigmatic expansion. While AIE-pharmacology addresses the specific subclass of drugs with AIE properties, fluoropharmacology emerges as the broader disciplinary framework encompassing all intrinsically luminescent drugs—regardless of whether they exhibit AIE, ACQ, or ARE behavior. The unifying principle is not the specific photophysical mechanism, but rather the fundamental premise that the drug molecule itself serves simultaneously as therapeutic agent and imaging probe.Thus, AIE-pharmacology can be understood as a crucial subdiscipline within the larger framework of fluoropharmacology—one that focuses on the ideal "turn-on" reporting mechanism provided by AIE drugs. Fluoropharmacology, in turn, provides the comprehensive theoretical architecture for studying, classifying, and therapeutically applying all intrinsically luminescent drugs based on their aggregation-dependent photophysical behaviors (ACQ, AIE, ARE). This expanded framework transforms our understanding from a narrow focus on a single phenomenon to a systematic discipline that recognizes the full spectrum of drug luminescence as a rich source of theranostic information.If AIE-pharmacology emphasizes "using AIE technology to study pharmacological problems," then fluoropharmacology goes a step further: it establishes "fluorescence" as an intrinsic property of the drug, rather than an external label. Fluoropharmacology is the scientific discipline that studies drug-biological system interactions through intrinsically fluorescent drugs, enabling real-time, multi-level visualization of pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics based on the "Drug-Probe Unity" concept and aggregation-dependent luminescent behaviors (ACQ, AIE, ARE). The core of this transformation lies in the design concept of "Drug-Probe Unity" (DPU).At the structural level, we propose Pharmacophore-Fluorophore Unity (PFU): the pharmacophore and fluorophore are no longer two independent modules but an inherent unity within the same molecular structure. This means molecular design no longer follows the "drug + fluorescent label" combination model, but rather discovers or designs molecules that inherently possess both pharmacological activity and AIE properties. The binary code of such molecules is defined by their aggregation-dependent luminescence: ACQ (1-0), AIE (0-1), ARE (1-1), or ARN (0-0). For fluoropharmacology, AIE (0-1) represents the optimal profile for target engagement reporting, while ARE (1-1) may be preferable for continuous tracking applications. Natural products such as vitexin belong to the AIE (0-1) category of intrinsic AIE drugs, as we have demonstrated in research on ferritin-nanocaged vitexin for treating asthenospermia, confirming its dual functionality with the characteristic 0-1 transition upon target engagement.At the functional level, we propose Drug-Probe Unity (DPU): the molecule serves both as a drug and as a contrast agent/fluorescent probe. This unity means that the therapeutic action and imaging function of the drug are no longer parallel or sequential relationships, but two aspects of the same molecular behavior. The process of the drug reaching the target and exerting its therapeutic effect is simultaneously the process of generating imaging signals; the intensity of efficacy and the intensity of signals are temporally and spatially correlated. The 0→1 transition serves as the intrinsic reporter of this process.At the application level, we propose Drug-Praxis Unity (DPU 2.0): from practice to practice; from the clinic to the clinic. Fluoropharmacology is not merely a laboratory research tool but should become a guiding theory for clinical practice. Through imaging monitoring, real-time adjustment of individualized dosing regimens can be achieved, ensuring that drugs reach and maintain optimal therapeutic concentrations at targets.This triple-unity philosophical architecture corresponds to a complete philosophical chain of ontology (what it is—the four luminescent states defining molecular identity), epistemology (how to know it—the 0-1 transition revealing drug action), and praxis (how to transform it—applying this knowledge to clinical practice), establishing fluoropharmacology as a disciplinary system with profound philosophical foundations.5 Dialogue and Distinction Between Photopharmacology and FluoropharmacologyWhen discussing the originality of fluoropharmacology, it is necessary to conduct a comparative analysis with photopharmacology.Photopharmacology is an emerging medical approach whose core involves introducing photoswitchable structures into pharmaceutical agents, using light irradiation to alter the shape and chemical properties of drugs, thereby modulating biological activity. The intellectual origins of this field can be traced back to Macht et al.'s discussions in 1926[60], with Meisel et al. formally proposing the concept of "photopharmacology" in 1980[61]. Its core advantage lies in achieving spatiotemporally precise control of drug activity and reducing off-target toxicity.Photopharmacology and fluoropharmacology share "light" as a core element, but their philosophical foundations and implementation paths differ fundamentally:Photopharmacology's core logic is "light control": the drug itself does not luminesce but possesses light responsiveness; light is applied externally as a control switch; efficacy is related to photocontrol but unrelated to imaging. Its goal is to achieve spatiotemporally precise drug activation through light.Fluoropharmacology's core logic is "self-luminescence": the drug itself luminesces (with a specific binary code: ACQ 1-0, AIE 0-1, ARE 1-1, or ARN 0-0); light is generated internally as a reporting signal; efficacy and imaging occur synchronously, mutually validating each other. Its goal is to achieve theranostics through luminescence, with the AIE (0-1) profile providing the ideal "turn-on" reporting mechanism.In brief, photopharmacology achieves precision therapy through "light control," while fluoropharmacology achieves theranostics through "self-luminescence."
