records.title: From Case Reports to Editorial Leadership: A Roadmap for Trainee Engagement in Academic Publishing
records.abstract: INTRODUCTION: WHY RESIDENT INVOLVEMENT MATTERS Publication represents a meaningful milestone during clinical training; one that signals scholarly engagement, intellectual growth, and entry into the academic community. Yet for many trainees, this goal can feel daunting, often perceived as reserved for a select few with prior research experience or established mentorship. Case reports, however, offer an accessible and impactful pathway for trainees at all levels to begin their publishing journey. The ACG Case Reports Journal (ACGCRJ) serves as a central platform where residents and fellows can develop foundational skills in scholarly writing, critical appraisal, and academic inquiry. Participation in case-based scholarship fosters intellectual curiosity, encourages thoughtful clinical reflection, and provides an early and tangible introduction to academic medicine during the formative years of training. Prior work has demonstrated that early exposure to scholarly activity is associated with sustained academic engagement later in one's career. Residents who produced above-average publications before residency had significantly higher publication output during both residency and fellowship (P < 0.001), and a higher number of publications during residency was independently associated with academic career placement (P = 0.002).1 Similarly, physicians who published as primary authors during training were significantly more likely to pursue academic medicine (odds ratio [OR] 1.25, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.0–1.5), and those who completed a fellowship had nearly 4 times the odds of an academic career compared with those who did not (OR 3.77, 95% CI: 2.0–7.2).2 The aim of this editorial is to demystify the case report publication process and provide a practical, trainee-focused framework for developing, writing, and submitting high-quality case reports to the ACGCRJ. By outlining common challenges and offering actionable strategies to overcome them, we seek to empower residents and fellows to engage confidently in scholarly activity, view publication as an attainable goal, and leverage case reports as a gateway to lifelong academic involvement. To provide structure for this discussion, we conceptualize trainee engagement in academic publishing along a four-stage continuum: Exposure, in which trainees encounter case-based scholarship and develop foundational writing skills through case report authorship; Participation, through active involvement in peer review and scholarly critique; Contribution, via sustained authorship, editorial roles, and academic output; and Leadership, through service on editorial boards, mentorship of junior trainees, and advocacy for an inclusive scholarly culture. This framework reflects the natural progression of academic development during residency and fellowship and serves as the organizational foundation for the guidance that follows. WRITING AND SUBMITTING CASE REPORTS: GETTING STARTED Below are the major steps for preparing and writing case report (Figure 1).Figure 1.: A stepwise approach to writing and submitting a case report.Step I: Identify a publishable case The first, and arguably most important, step in writing a case report is selecting an appropriate and compelling case.3 Successful authors should focus on cases that pique their own intellectual curiosity while also considering characteristics that have historically been associated with publishable case reports.4,5 These include: Rare diseases or uncommon clinical entities. Novel presentations or atypical manifestations of common diseases. Unique or illustrative imaging, endoscopic findings, or procedural videos. Noteworthy adverse effects or unexpected therapeutic benefits of medications. Step II: Conduct a focused literature review Once a case of interest is identified, effective preparation begins with a thorough and focused review of the existing literature. This process should be guided by a clearly defined question related to the disease itself, a distinctive feature of the case, or the specific clinical context it highlights.4,6 Authors should prioritize high-quality, peer-reviewed sources using databases such as PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, or Google Scholar. Careful documentation and organization of references at this stage facilitate accurate citation and coherent synthesis during manuscript development. Step III: Define the central message and learning points Equally important is clarifying the educational message of the case report. Authors should articulate clear learning points that anchor the narrative and guide the reader. These may address disease pathophysiology, diagnostic challenges, therapeutic decision-making, management strategies, or broader lessons in clinical reasoning and judgment.7 A focused message helps distinguish high-quality case reports from purely descriptive narratives. Step IV: Craft a clear clinical narrative Beyond identifying learning points and selecting figures, authors should focus on constructing a coherent and engaging clinical narrative. A strong case report tells a focused story: presenting the clinical problem, outlining the diagnostic reasoning, highlighting key decision points, and explaining how the case adds to existing knowledge. Avoid exhaustive timelines or unnecessary laboratory data; instead, emphasize information that directly supports the central message. Clear narration helps readers follow the clinical reasoning process and enhances the educational impact of the case. Step V: Select impactful figures Figures play a critical role in enhancing the educational value of case reports. High-quality endoscopic images, radiographic studies, and histopathologic findings can substantially strengthen a submission when they directly support the teaching objectives of the case.5 Figures should be carefully selected, appropriately annotated when necessary, and accompanied by concise legends that reinforce—rather than repeat—the key learning points. Step VI: Choose the appropriate submission format In addition to traditional case reports, the ACGCRJ offers an image-based submission format that highlights unique and educational endoscopic, radiographic, or histopathologic findings with minimal accompanying narrative. The journal also accepts video-based submissions, which are particularly well suited for demonstrating dynamic endoscopic techniques, procedural nuances, and visually instructive findings. Developing skills in video editing can be an invaluable part of this process, allowing trainees to effectively present cases, enhance visual storytelling, and share educational content with the broader GI community—while also contributing to personal growth and academic skill development. This option provides an excellent entry point for trainees, particularly those early in training, to engage in scholarly activity while developing skills in visual diagnosis and concise teaching. Image submissions are especially well suited for cases in which the primary educational value lies in the visual findings rather than an extensive clinical discussion. Step VII: Prepare for submission Authors should address practical considerations early in the process, including obtaining patient consent when required, ensuring complete deidentification of clinical data and images, and reviewing journal-specific submission guidelines before writing. Developing a clear outline aligned with the journal's structure can streamline manuscript preparation and reduce unnecessary revisions. Limitations of case reports Beyond procedural preparation, aspiring authors should also approach case report writing with a clear-eyed appreciation of the format's inherent limitations. While case reports offer an accessible and impactful entry point into academic publishing, trainees and reviewers alike should remain mindful of their intrinsic constraints. As a study design, case reports occupy the lower rungs of the evidence hierarchy, providing observational snapshots that cannot establish causality or be generalized beyond the individual patient. They are therefore best understood as hypothesis-generating contributions rather than definitive evidence. In addition, the publication landscape for case reports is susceptible to novelty bias, wherein unusual or dramatic presentations are disproportionately accepted, while informative negative outcomes or common disease manifestations with atypical features may receive less attention; a dynamic that can skew the cumulative literature. Considerations concerning equity also warrant acknowledgment: access to scholarly mentorship, protected academic time, and institutional infrastructure for research varies considerably across training programs, potentially disadvantaging trainees at community or underresourced programs. Recognizing these structural barriers is essential to fostering a more inclusive and representative academic publishing culture. Awareness of these limitations does not diminish the value of case-based scholarship; rather, it reflects the critical appraisal that defines a thoughtful and responsible clinician-scholar. Common pitfalls and practical solutions Common pitfalls in case report writing include poor case selection, unfocused narratives with excessive or irrelevant detail, suboptimal image quality, and overinterpretation of findings beyond the available evidence.8 Many of these challenges can be mitigated through comprehensive literature review, early clarification of the case's educational message, and supervision from experienced authors. Familiarity with previously published articles in the ACGCRJ can further help trainees develop an understanding of effective structure, scope, and scholarly tone. BECOMING A PEER REVIEWER AS A RESIDENT Peer review is a foundational component of academic medicine and an important avenue through which residents can actively engage in scholarly discourse. For medical trainees, peer review involves evaluating submitted work, providing constructive and thoughtful feedback, and assessing whether manuscripts meet appropriate educational and scientific standards. Participation in the peer-review process offers numerous benefits during training and early academic careers, including improvement in scientific writing, enhanced critical appraisal skills, and development of effective communication and teaching abilities.9 In addition, peer review fosters professionalism, collegiality, and a sense of belonging within the academic community. For many residents, involvement in peer review and academic scholarship may initially feel intimidating. However, several accessible pathways exist for trainees interested in becoming peer reviewers. Identifying a mentor represents a critical first step. When goals and interests align, experienced mentors can provide guidance in manuscript evaluation, scientific reasoning, and ethical responsibilities inherent to peer review, while offering early exposure to the review process.10 Beyond mentorship-based opportunities, residents may also pursue direct involvement with the ACGCRJ. As a journal specifically designed for trainees, ACGCRJ actively encourages residents and fellows to participate in peer review. Interested individuals may register as reviewers through Editorial Manager, the journal's official submission and review platform, or contact the editorial office directly to express interest. This inclusive approach lowers traditional barriers to entry and allows motivated trainees to contribute meaningfully to the academic mission of the journal. What makes a great trainee reviewer Effective trainee reviewers share several key attributes that enhance both the quality of reviews and the educational experience for authors11: Constructive and respectful tone, emphasizing improvement rather than criticism. Focus on educational value, particularly clarity of learning points and clinical relevance. Attention to structure and organization, including logical flow and adherence to journal guidelines. Critical appraisal grounded in evidence, with suggestions supported by literature when appropriate. Specific and actionable feedback, avoiding vague or generic comments. Awareness of scope, recognizing when revisions are feasible vs when limitations are inherent. Commitment to timeliness, respecting authors' efforts and editorial workflows. Exceptional reviewer contributions may be formally recognized through honors such as the ACGCRJ Reviewer of the Month award, highlighting outstanding commitment to trainee-led peer review. In addition, participation in the review process fosters the development of critical appraisal and scholarly writing skills and provides valuable opportunities to connect with editorial board members, reinforcing peer review as a skill set that can be learned, refined, and applied throughout an academic career. Ethical considerations in peer review Ethical conduct is central to the integrity of the peer-review process. Trainee reviewers must maintain strict confidentiality of all submitted materials and should not share manuscripts, images, or data outside the review process. Potential conflicts of interest—including personal, professional, or institutional relationships with authors or subject matter—should be disclosed promptly to the editorial team. Reviewers should provide objective, unbiased assessments and avoid using privileged information gained through peer review for personal or academic advantage. In addition, reviewers should exercise caution in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools during peer review. Manuscripts or portions of submitted content should not be copied, uploaded, or shared with AI platforms in a manner that compromises confidentiality or intellectual property. When permitted by journal policy, AI tools may be used only in a limited and responsible manner, such as for general language refinement, without reproducing or disclosing manuscript content. EDITORIAL AND LEADERSHIP OPPORTUNITIES Trainees can gain access to a broad range of editorial and leadership opportunities at ACGCRJ. The ACGCRJ is distinctive in that it is edited exclusively by gastroenterology fellows, creating a uniquely trainee-driven and supervised environment for developing editorial judgment, advanced critical appraisal skills, and academic leadership. Service on the editorial board offers structured exposure to manuscript decision making and the inner workings of academic publishing.12 In addition to editorial board roles, the journal expanded leadership opportunities for internal medicine residents with the introduction of a dedicated Social Media Ambassador role in 2025. In this capacity, residents collaborate closely with the Editorial Board to disseminate published cases, podcasts, and “Image of the Month” features across professional social media platforms, including X (formerly Twitter) and LinkedIn. This role allows residents to cultivate a professional gastroenterology-focused digital presence, demonstrate early leadership and academic engagement, and gain visibility within the GI community before fellowship training. Moreover, it supports the translation of complex clinical and public health information into accessible educational content for broader audiences.13 To position oneself for success in editorial and leadership roles, several foundational principles are essential. As with any scholarly endeavor, consistent engagement and deliberate practice are key to skill development. Attention to detail, professionalism in communication, reliability, and adherence to deadlines are critical attributes of effective reviewers and editors and are often factors considered for advancement and recognition, including honors such as Reviewer of the Month. Sustained involvement with journals such as the ACGCRJ also facilitates the development of enduring professional relationships in national societies such as American College of Gastroenterology. Many trainees participate in formal mentorship structures in which they are paired with senior editors who provide longitudinal guidance on career development, advanced fellowship training, and academic opportunities that extend beyond the editorial term. In addition, service on a national trainee-led editorial board fosters a unique sense of camaraderie among motivated residents and fellows across institutions. These connections frequently evolve into long-term collaborations, with peers becoming future colleagues, coinvestigators, and trusted academic partners throughout one's career. PRACTICAL ADVICE FOR BALANCING RESIDENCY AND SCHOLARSHIP During residency, trainees must continuously balance the demands of patient care with research and other scholarly activities. Limited time and competing clinical responsibilities are among the most frequently cited barriers to sustained academic engagement.14,15 Survey data confirm the breadth of these barriers: in a study of 57 medical trainees, time constraints, insufficient statistical and methodology training, competing educational commitments, and inadequate incentives were the most commonly cited obstacles to research participation.15 Yet despite these challenges, most respondents expressed genuine interest in engaging in scholarly activity, with increased funding and institutional incentives identified as the most impactful facilitators. These perceived obstacles can discourage otherwise motivated trainees from pursuing scholarly work. Residents who successfully participate in scholarly work despite these constraints often view academic activity not as an added burden, but as an integrated and purposeful component of their clinical training. At the individual level, residents who engage consistently in scholarship can achieve meaningful output, with a qualitative study showing that 93% produced peer-reviewed publications and many presented at regional (79%) and national (64%) levels.16 Strategic time management plays a central role in maintaining this balance. Coordinating scholarly efforts over time and setting aside brief, regular blocks dedicated to writing or manuscript review have been associated with increased and more sustained research productivity among residents.17 Establishing realistic and clearly defined goals further supports this approach. Rather than pursuing multiple projects simultaneously, residents often achieve greater success by focusing on a single, well-scoped scholarly task, which promotes follow-through and reduces cognitive overload. This strategy aligns with cognitive load theory, which demonstrates that excessive simultaneous demands impair learning and task performance.18 Importantly, many scholarly contributions arise directly from routine patient care. Clinical encounters characterized by diagnostic uncertainty, atypical presentations, or unexpected outcomes frequently serve as the foundation for case reports and other academic work. With early mentorship and timely, organized documentation, these observations can be efficiently transformed into meaningful and publishable scholarship.16 CONCLUSION As outlined through the 4-stage continuum of exposure, participation, contribution, and leadership, residents at every stage of training have meaningful opportunities to engage in scholarly activity. Scholarly engagement may begin early in residency through case report authorship, evolve into participation in peer review, and ultimately extend to editorial and leadership roles that foster professional growth and academic development. Approaching scholarship through small, clearly defined projects and viewing journal involvement as a longitudinal learning process allows residents to build confidence, practical skills, and a scholarly identity while maintaining the demands of clinical training. As a resident-driven and fellow-driven journal, the ACGCRJ provides an accessible and supportive entry point into academic publishing, empowering trainees to develop essential academic skills while opening pathways toward fellowship training and long-term engagement in academic medicine. records.title: From challenge-skills balance to wellbeing in sports: the role of team identification and flow
records.abstract: This study investigated the psychological mechanisms linking challenge-skills balance to psychological wellbeing among team-sport athletes, considering team identification and flow experience as the fundamental drivers of this relationship. A sample of 281 team-sport athletes completed an online survey comprising measures of challenge-skill balance, team identification, flow, and wellbeing. Results supported the hypothesized model: Athletes who perceived their competencies as congruent with competitive demands reported stronger team identification, which in turn was related to deeper flow experiences. Flow was then associated with wellbeing, mediating the effect of team identification. These findings highlight the interconnected role of cognitive resources, social identity processes, and optimal experiential states in sustaining athletes' psychological wellbeing.

records.title: From molecule to bedside and back: the integration of computational and experimental physiology in the digital age
records.abstract: Historically, physiology has evolved from observational descriptions to the rigorous dissection of mechanisms. Today, we witness another transformation where experimental and computational methodologies are no longer separate disciplines, but rather interconnected strategies that are essential for navigating the nonlinear complexity of the heart. This Special Issue represents a maturation of the ‘Physiome Project’ vision (Loewe et al.; 2025): a quantitative, multi-scale description of physiological dynamics, now spanning from the metabolic state of a crossbridge to the haemodynamic flow in a fibrillating atrium. The contributions in this collection largely stem from the Cardiac Physiome Workshop 2024 in Freiburg, Germany. There, the community gathered to discuss the bidirectional crosstalk between theoretical foundations and specific clinical challenges, such as atrial fibrillation and drug safety. Indeed, we see a broadening of the use of models, which become predictive engines capable of exploring the design of novel therapies, the assessment of clinical risks in real time, and the scaling of physiology from molecule to organ. Thus, successful physiological insights now emerge from the iterative feedback between laboratory data and mathematical reconstruction. The interdisciplinary methodological frameworks highlighting this integration have been reviewed by Yang & Sobie (2025), who focus on defining the essential ‘ingredients’ for the effective integration of computational and experimental approaches. A central, recurring theme in this issue is the emergence of the digital twin. While this term is often used to describe patient-specific modelling in a clinical setting, several contributions in this collection emphasise that the concept also encompasses fundamental biophysical models. These mechanistic twins, though perhaps not tailored to a single individual, provide the necessary framework to interpret experimental variability and define the evolutionary robustness of cardiac function. This integration is crucially bidirectional: while computational models predict outcomes, high-resolution experimental and clinical mapping remains the basis that informs and constrains the next generation of in silico studies. In a seminal contribution, Noble (2026a) traces the theoretical foundations of our current understanding of cardiac rhythm and the models we use to simulate it. By reflecting on the evolution of pacemaker models, Noble demonstrates how mathematical frameworks did not just follow experimental discovery but often pointed toward the necessary experimental questions. This work is further contextualised by Maltsev et al. (2026), whose perspective highlights the evolutionary robustness of these physiological systems, which is a concept essential for understanding why certain rhythms persist or fail under pathological stress. The ongoing dialogue in this field is further reinforced by the commentary of Noble (2026b), which reminds us that, as our models become more complex, we must remain grounded in the fundamental biophysical principles that govern cardiac automaticity. Atrial fibrillation (AF) remains the most common sustained arrhythmia and its structural basis and maintenance mechanisms remain subjects of intense investigation. A major challenge in treating AF is the scale mismatch between the microscopic environment, where triggers arise, and the macroscopic mapping performed in clinical electrophysiology laboratories. Several works in this Special Issue explore how new high-resolution imaging and computational reconstruction technologies are bridging this divide, moving the field towards a more nuanced understanding of how structure influences function. Kulathilaka et al. (2026) exemplify the importance of atrial microstructure by implementing digital models derived from micron-resolution imaging of the human heart. They demonstrate that re-entrant drivers are not randomly distributed but are anchored to specific microstructural features. In an accompanying Perspective, Potse (2026) discusses how these findings suggest that AF drivers ‘like to live in narrow spots’, effectively linking the multiple wavelet and rotor hypotheses by showing how chaotic activity can be organised by anatomical constraints. This microstructural analysis is further explored in a Journal Club article by Cutler (2026), who examines the transition from microstructure to arrhythmia and the specific structural drivers that sustain re-entrant activity. Complementing these ex vivo insights, Horrach et al. (2026) provide a translational review of mapping techniques for evaluating fibrosis in patients. They discuss how various imaging modalities, beyond standard electroanatomic mapping, can characterise the pathological substrate in vivo, thereby bridging the gap between high-resolution histology and clinical catheter ablation. Beyond fixed structural obstacles, the dynamic, functional remodelling of ion channels provides a secondary, evolving substrate for arrhythmia. Meier et al. (2026) applied computational modelling to explore the rate-dependent trafficking of small-conductance calcium-activated potassium (SK) channels. The collection also points out that AF is not solely an electrical phenomenon but one with profound haemodynamic consequences. Bäck et al. (2026) demonstrate how virtual interventions, such as left atrial appendage occlusion, can predict improvements in blood flow and reduce stasis risk, offering a tool for pre-procedural planning. This work is discussed by Hassan et al. (2026). Perhaps the most direct clinical application of these ‘digital heart’ tools is seen in the prospective in silico trial by Dasí et al. (2026). By simulating drug effects across a population of models representing inter-individual variability, they identified combined SK and two-pore-domain potassium channel blockade as a potentially effective strategy for AF cardioversion. This approach illustrates how computational physiology can ‘de-risk’ pharmaceutical development by identifying synergistic targets and predicting outcomes before a single patient is enrolled in a trial. This approach further supports the translational promise of targeting the SK channel, as comprehensively reviewed by Zheng et al. (2026). In the ventricles, the focus shifts to the subtle interplay between activation sequences, repolarisation heterogeneity, and arrhythmia vulnerability. Refining the interpretation of non-invasive data, Smits et al. (2026) present evidence contrary to the assumption that late-activated regions always display shortened action potential durations to maintain T-wave concordance. To correctly interpret electrocardiographic imaging maps in patients with heart failure, they propose a computational strategy challenging longstanding clinical assumptions. The connection between physiological gradients and arrhythmia risk is further explored by Sobota et al. (2026), who show that the apicobasal repolarisation gradient diminishes or inverts with age. This loss of the natural gradient may paradoxically increase vulnerability to re-entrant arrhythmias, providing a potential mechanistic link between the ageing process and the broader societal challenge of managing arrhythmic risk in an increasingly ageing population. In safety pharmacology, models are proving increasingly valuable for predicting cardiotoxicity and minimising the risks associated with specific therapies. Villar-Valero et al. (2026) present a parametric study using three-dimensional (3D) magnetic resonance imaging-based models to predict the effects of doxorubicin. By computationally modelling the specific patterns of diffuse interstitial fibrosis induced by the drug, they identify this structural remodelling as a key biomarker that promotes conduction block. As noted by Durço et al. (2026) in the accompanying Journal Club, this illustrates how the passive collagen network dictates the propagation of electrical waves. Chabiniok & Zaha (2026) expand upon this theme by reviewing the application of cardiac digital twins in assessing chemotherapy-induced substrates. Mora et al. (2026) apply electromechanical simulations to assess the effectiveness of omecamtiv mecarbil in treating heart failure. As discussed by Malicki et al. (2025), this approach offers a well-controlled in silico environment to dissect drug effects in the absence of other systemic influences. The link between metabolism and mechanics is a critical determinant of dysfunction in conditions such as diabetic cardiomyopathy. Musgrave et al. (2026) address this phenomenon with metabolite-sensitive crossbridge models to investigate how the metabolic environment in diabetes directly alters myofilament energetics and stiffness. Such models are important in providing a rigorous thermodynamic framework to explain how changes in metabolite concentrations, often seen in diabetes, impact muscle mechanoenergetics at the molecular level. Complementing this subcellular perspective, Bertrand et al. (2026) review cardiac remodelling in type 2 diabetes across multiple scales, discussing how computational multiscale modelling can link these subcellular defects with tissue-level fibrosis and autonomic neuropathy, thereby improving our understanding of disease progression. At the cellular level, Folkmanaite et al. (2026) demonstrate the value of computational approaches by utilising electromechanical modelling of human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes to predict drug-induced contractility effects. In structural heart disease, Dvoulety & Sitina (2026) propose a haemodynamic–energetic mechanism for sudden cardiac death in aortic stenosis. Their model describes a state of ‘cardiac stalling’, whereby the energy demand of the hypertrophied ventricle exceeds the supply during stress, leading to mechanical failure. Townsend (2026) emphasises that this energy-balance framework explains syncope that purely hydraulic models may miss, pointing out the ability of models to assess catastrophic events in silico that cannot be ethically induced in human subjects. Moreover, models are increasingly capable of predicting long-term structural adaptation. Sharifi et al. (2026) incorporated multiscale finite element modelling to elucidate the role of the baroreflex feedback loop in ventricular growth, connecting neural control to tissue mechanics. Moscoloni et al. (2026) further recognise the significance of considering biological variables frequently disregarded in generic models: sex alone explains at least 25% of ventricular morphological variability. These fundamental shape disparities between male and female hearts should be incorporated into future patient-specific or sex-specific simulations. Finally, the developmental origins of these conditions are explored by Bueno-Palomeque et al. (2026), who use a synthesis of clinical and computational data to characterise preadolescents born with intrauterine growth restriction. Moving from pharmacological triggers to structural substrates, this work demonstrates how multi-scale modelling can isolate the specific contributions of ionic remodelling to the developing heart, reinforcing the ‘developmental origins of health and disease’ hypothesis. The boundary at the interface between biological and digital systems is becoming increasingly blurred, creating fertile ground for the integration of bioelectronics and artificial intelligence. Stark et al. (2026) review the development of flexible, implantable systems that utilise real-time data processing to close the loop between sensing and therapeutic intervention. These autonomous, closed-loop bioelectronic platforms are capable of sensing and modulating cardiac function in real time and represent an advancement in translational computational physiology. Technological progress in this area is supported by the development of sophisticated cellular-level models, such as the voltage-modulated Markov chain model for the Piezo1 ion channel presented by Ogiermann et al. (2026). By refining our ability to simulate mechanotransduction, such models provide the biophysical foundation for the next generation of intelligent, mechanosensitive devices. Furthermore, Greiner et al. (2025) introduce a deep learning-enabled toolkit for the automated 3D segmentation of ventricular cardiomyocytes to build these models at scale, effectively removing the manual bottleneck in high-resolution structural reconstruction. Physiological principles are tested and validated further at the extremes of environmental stress. Tripoli et al. (2026) used multiscale models to assess cardiac function across the spectrum from microgravity to hypergravity, informing spaceflight medicine and our fundamental understanding of gravitational adaptation. As Collia et al. (2026) note in an accompanying Perspective, these simulations allow us to explore physiological states that cannot be replicated in standard laboratory settings, offering a unique perspective on the robustness of cardiac function. Finally, comparative physiology continues to provide essential evolutionary benchmarks for identifying conserved mechanisms of cardiac automaticity and regeneration. This collection includes a novel mathematical model of the zebrafish ventricular action potential by Cestariolo et al. (2026), delivering a quantitative framework for this increasingly popular model of cardiac development. In the sinoatrial node, Linder et al. (2026) examine how sympathetic stimulation can compensate for hypocalcaemia-induced bradycardia. By comparing human and rabbit cells, they identify fundamental mechanisms of pacemaking robustness that are conserved across species as well as noable differences, thereby further grounding our computational reconstructions in comparative biological reality. The reliability of any computational model is inherently linked to the quality and resolution of the experimental data used for its construction and validation. As the complexity of simulations increases, so too does the requirement for highly accurate ground-truth datasets for parametrisation and validation. This collection showcases significant advancements in integrated experimental setups that allow for the comprehensive analysis of cardiac function across scales. Siles et al. (2026) describe a sophisticated platform for integrated panoramic optical and electrical mapping, enabling detailed arrhythmia studies in isolated hearts with high spatial and temporal resolution. This approach provides the necessary validation data for complex 3D ventricular models, a topic expanded upon by Zgierski-Johnston & Huisken (2025). They discuss the profound implications of being able to ‘see’ the heart in 3D in order to analyse the mechanical and electrical drivers of arrhythmia. However, even the most advanced experimental data are subject to variability and measurement error. Acknowledging that data is never ‘perfect’, Tanner et al. (2026) present a rigorous framework for uncertainty quantification in cardiac modelling. Focusing specifically on myocardial fibre orientation and activation patterns, they argue that incorporating error bars into simulation predictions is not simply a statistical exercise but a fundamental requirement for establishing the reliability and clinical safety of in silico results. By treating parameter uncertainty with the same rigour as experimental error, the research community can move towards more robust, reproducible, and ultimately translatable predictive models. The papers collected in this Special Issue demonstrate that computational physiology has evolved from a niche subdiscipline into a central pillar of modern cardiovascular research. The ability to integrate experimental data and computational simulations, spanning the scale from the molecular energetics of a crossbridge to the complex haemodynamic flows of a fibrillating atrium, is now a reality, not a distant aspiration. This convergence is accelerating the translation of fundamental physiological principles into clinical understanding and, ultimately, novel therapeutic strategies. As we look to the future, several key themes have emerged as priorities for the community. The first of these is the continued refinement and precise application of digital twin technology. While patient-specific modelling shows great potential for precision medicine, the contributions in this issue remind us that digital twins of in vitro experiments and generic mechanistic models, which explain fundamental biological principles, remain indispensable for interpreting experimental variability and defining the evolutionary robustness of cardiac function. Secondly, high-resolution, multi-modal experimental optical, ultrasound, and structural mapping must remain at the core of our field. This collection highlights that the next generation of in silico tools will only be as robust as the experimental data used to constrain them. Additionally, as our models move closer to the bedside, a rigorous commitment to uncertainty quantification and the inclusion of biological diversity, including age, sex, and developmental origins, is no longer optional; it is a key requirement for clinical safety and efficacy. Furthermore, the integration of machine learning and bioelectronics is enhancing our ability to reconstruct cardiac structure and modulate function in real time. The adoption of automated image analysis and autonomous closed-loop systems represents a practical shift towards more responsive physiological monitoring that remains grounded in the biophysical reality of the heart as a complex multicellular network. We hope that this Special Issue serves as both a comprehensive resource for the current community and a catalyst for the next generation of researchers. By continuing to close the gap between the analogue world and its digital representation, we can ensure that cardiac physiology remains at the forefront of the quest to understand, diagnose, treat, and ultimately prevent cardiovascular disease. records.title: From Sensors to Decisions in an Undergraduate e-Logistics Course
records.venue: 2025 5th International Conference on Intelligent Cybernetics Technology & Applications (ICICyTA)
records.abstract: This paper reports a low-cost, hands-on intervention in an undergraduate e-Logistics course that introduces digital logistics through simple Internet-of-Things prototyping. Across eight weeks, twenty-one students built basic tools for inventory and warehouse tasks using microcontrollers, entry-level sensors, MQTT connectivity, and cloud dashboards. The design mirrored small and medium-sized enterprise conditions by keeping kit costs near USD10, using simple classroom layouts, and relying on campus Wi-Fi. Brief instruction allowed students to make concrete design choices, wire devices, publish data, visualize signals, and iterate on placement and thresholds. Qualitative responses show strong perceived learning gains: 83 % highlighted meaningful sensor and hardware understanding, 78 % stated that project-based learning improved comprehension compared with lectures, and 72% felt more prepared for real logistics environments. Analysis of artifacts, dashboards, and reflections indicates improved articulation of logistics concepts, problem-solving under constraints, and digital literacy, alongside clearer awareness of how cost, layout, and signal quality influence feasible SME-oriented solutions. Privacy and safety practices were applied through credentialed topics, non-identifying pay-loads, and anonymized imagery. The structured telemetry and short decision notes produced by students form AI-ready traces suitable for future exercises such as anomaly detection or simple forecasting. The paper concludes with guidance for kit reuse and classroom operations, supporting transferability to inventory, warehousing, and introductory automation courses.

records.title: Gamification and AI-Powered Training Models for Cybersecurity Awareness and Skill Development
records.abstract: The human-centricity of defense continues to pose a severe threat to contemporary digital infrastructures because of the fixed instructional framework and sluggish skills validation. In this paper, CASCADES (Cognitive-Adaptive Scenario Construction and Dynamic Evaluation System), which is an integrated system of intelligence-based structures ensuring that user preparedness is jointly promoted in a framework that would improve in real-time competence representations. The proposed approach has an advantage over traditional methods that can be based on predetermined content and progression through rewards, but introduces the ability to dynamically synthesize operational scenarios in connection with the specific behavioral patterns, response consistency and cognitive load tolerance. CASCADES uses a closed loop learning design whereby the actions taken by the participants of the system are examined to draw conclusions about the latent states of the capabilities which in turn can be used to make timely modifications in the level of challenge of a task or the level of difficulty of a situation. Hybrid learning engine combines the sequential decision modeling, and policy optimization in order to predict the error tendencies and introduce fixative cues into simulated environment. The temporal resilience index measures skill development based on the efficiency in recovery, adaptation in the face of perturbation and long-term retention, instead of short-term gains in performance. The proposed framework is experimentally shown to maintain engagement and significantly enhance adaptive reasoning and procedural robustness that are largely not user profile dependent. The findings reveal that CASCADES is a successful knowledge decay reduction and overfitting to routine tasks mitigation strategy that is scalable and resilient to enhance capability ongoing improvement capabilities in changing threat environments. The suggested method attains an overall accuracy of 94.6%, indicating consistent and dependable decision-making performance throughout dynamic interaction settings.

records.title: Gamification as a Curriculum Strategy: Effects on Mathematics Performance and Anxiety in Relation to Intelligence Types
records.abstract: Download PDF Article Download Graphical Abstract Gamification as a Curriculum Strategy: Effects on Mathematics Performance and Anxiety in Relation to Intelligence Types Abstract This study examines the correlation between the performance of primary school students following a gamification-based mathematics curriculum and their levels of anxiety during mathematics lessons, considering individual differences in intelligence types. The theoretical framework highlights the most important empirical studies that analyse the extent to which gamified interventions reduce anxiety. In addition, it emphasises the methodology for structuring a curricular educational programme centred on gamification as a complex educational strategy to promote specific values, attitudes, and behaviours. The quasi-experimental design involved a control and an experimental group, both of which were each subjected to a one-month curricular educational programme. Specifically, the experimental group's programme assumes solving didactic tasks related to the curricular content exclusively through gamification. Furthermore, the effect of gamification on school anxiety, moderated by the levels of logico-mathematical and intrapersonal intelligence, was also studied. The results of study indicated that statistically significant correlation existed between school-level efficiency and students' anxiety but the levels of intelligence did not moderate this correlation. Overall, the study highlighted that a school environment focused on the specific advantages of using gamification has direct effects through modelling an efficient learning environment, increasing the ability to understand mathematical phenomena, and decreasing anxiety regarding assessment situations in mathematics (operationalised by the McKenzie, Multiple Intelligences Inventory), without being statistically significantly moderated by logical-mathematical or intrapersonal intelligence levels. Keywords Gamification, Scratch Programming, Mathematics Anxiety, Assessment in Mathematics, Creative Problem-Solving JEL Classification I2 1. Introduction In this study, we began with an experimental design based on a curricular educational programme to introduce students to a formal environment focused on gamification, aiming to promote growth in school mathematics performance. This research direction is supported by the fact that, if properly implemented, a correctly-structured curriculum focused on elementary mathematics in primary education can have a significant impact on students’ future academic performance (Fadlelmula, 2022). Moreover, the construction of a curricular educational programme is increasingly used in modern educational experiences, particularly in subject-specific structuring of mathematics contents (Havârneanu, 2022), as active learning is stimulated when teachers adopt innovative approaches to teaching mathematics (Taranto et al., 2021). One of these strategies' innovative approaches is gamification (Jutin & Maat, 2024), which helps students become more creative in problem-solving (Havârneanu, 2013). At the same time, it develops their critical thinking both as a process of intentional evaluation of problem data and as a process of logical inference (Halpern, 2014). While gamification has been increasingly applied in educational contexts, there is still limited evidence regarding its structured integration into mathematics curricula at the early primary level. Many studies address gamification as an isolated activity or a classroom practice, but fewer have examined its systematic inclusion within a curricular framework designed to strengthen foundational mathematical skills. This study addresses this gap by evaluating the effectiveness of a gamification-based curricular programme designed explicitly for elementary mathematics education. The main objective of this study is to investigate whether the implementation of a gamified curricular educational programme can improve students’ mathematics performance in primary school. Specifically, the research aims to examine the extent to which gamification promotes active engagement, problem-solving creativity, and critical thinking in young learners. This research was conducted using an experimental design, with students divided into two groups: an experimental group that received mathematics instruction through the gamified curricular programme and a control group that followed traditional teaching methods. Data were collected from classroom assessments, standardised mathematics tests, and structured observations over the course of the intervention. The analysis focused on comparing performance outcomes between the two groups to assess the impact of the gamified approach. The participants in the study were primary school students, who are legally considered minors. For this reason, strict ethical guidelines were followed throughout the research process. Prior informed consent was obtained from parents or legal guardians, and assent was secured from the children themselves. The study was conducted in accordance with ethical standards for educational research, ensuring anonymity, confidentiality of student data, and the right to withdraw from the study at any time. The findings of this study are particularly relevant for multiple stakeholders in education. Primary school teachers can benefit by adopting gamification strategies that foster student engagement, reduce mathematics-related anxiety, and support the development of problem-solving skills. Curriculum designers and policymakers can draw on these results to integrate gamification elements into structured educational programmes, ensuring that technology-supported methods such as Scratch are embedded systematically rather than used sporadically. Teacher trainers may also use these findings to prepare educators with practical tools to address math anxiety in early learners. Finally, parents and students stand to benefit indirectly, as gamified environments not only improve performance but also create psychologically safer and more motivating conditions for learning mathematics. By systematically incorporating gamification into curricula, schools can create effective, student-centred environments that foster resilience, alleviate test anxiety, and improve long-term academic outcomes. Mathematics assessment has long been identified as a significant source of student anxiety, particularly in primary education. Test-related stress can undermine performance, reduce self-efficacy, and negatively influence long-term attitudes toward mathematics. In this context, gamification has emerged as a promising pedagogical approach to reduce anxiety and foster more positive learning environments. Our study provides further evidence that Scratch-based gamification can alleviate several forms of mathematics-related anxiety, including fears of self-expression, social stress, and teacher-related anxiety, while simultaneously improving test performance. These findings are consistent with previous research, which has shown that gamification enhances motivation and reduces negative emotions in learning contexts. Hamari et al. (2016) demonstrated that challenging yet playful environments foster engagement and flow, while Su and Cheng (2015) found that gamified tasks improved student motivation and reduced avoidance behaviours in assessments. Our results extend these insights by showing that gamified interventions not only increase engagement but can also directly reduce anxiety linked to mathematics testing. records.title: Gamification vs.  Game-Based Learning: Differential Effects on Student Motivation in STEM  Classroo
records.abstract: Thus, student motivation in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) is a chronic problem, encouraging educators to include game elements in the allocated instruction. But two separate methodologies, gamification (adding elements from games, like points and badges, to non-game contexts) and game-based learning (employing full-bore games as the primary learning vehicle), are often confused with one another in both practice and research. This study aims to differentiate the effects of these factors on student motivation in secondary STEM classrooms. We will use a quasi-experimental design within six middle school science classes (N = 144). Three classes will receive a gamified adaptation of the standard curriculum, while three other classes will interact with a purpose-built educational game covering the same learning objectives. A control group will be taught traditionally. Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) will be administered pre- and post-intervention; additional qualitative data will be collected via semi-structured interviews. While both interventions are expected to lead to better motivation than conventional instruction, it is hypothesised that game-based learning will have a greater positive impact on intrinsic motivation and situational interest owing to its immersive narrative and authentic problem-solving contexts. On the other hand, gamification is believed to hold a more prominent role when it comes to extrinsic motivation and achieving task completion in the short run. Results will provide empirical guidance/useful case evidence for educators and instructional designers determining when to implement which game-informed strategies in order to facilitate sustained engagement in STEM.IntroductionBackgroundThe continuous drop in student motivation has been identified as a major concern for educators and policymakers around the world within science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) classrooms [1]. Although STEM literacy is considered essential for economic competitiveness, innovative minds in workforce development [1], surveys of students consistently show that interest in subject areas related to STEM declines markedly during the middle and secondary school years [2]. Traditional teaching methods, which typically involve lecture-style transmission of information and pre-packaged problem sets divorced from real-world context, often do not satisfy the basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness, three elements described in self-determination theory as essential for intrinsic motivation [3]. To address this motivational crisis, educators have increasingly adopted game-informed pedagogies [4]. The premise is solid: Digital games are carefully crafted to ensure abiding interest through challenge, feedback, narrative, and agency elements that closely map onto principles of effective learning spaces [5]. As a result, two different but often conflated strategies emerged: gamification, incorporating game-design elements such as points, badges, and leaderboards into non-game education [5], and Game-Based Learning (GBL): using full-blown games as the main vehicle for delivering content and getting students to practice skills [6]. The proliferation of these approaches mirrors a wider trend towards learner-centred, interactive pedagogies; the lack of conceptual clarity about their specific mechanisms is an ongoing challenge for both research and practice.Problem StatementAlthough gamification and game-based learning can rely on a similar foundation of game-inspired design, they are in fact two distinct instructional strategies grounded in different psychological and pedagogical mechanisms [7]. Gamification works by applying motivational affordances to preexisting curricular content, usually making use of extrinsic motivators to help ensure completion of tasks and compliance with desirable behaviours [8]. In contrast, game-based learning embeds the outcome objectives within the core mechanics and thematic structure of a game, striving to create intrinsic motivation through immersion, problem-solving, and authentic contextualization [9]. Despite these theoretical differences, educational literature as well as classroom practice often use the two terms interchangeably, leading to what some scholars have called “conceptual slippage” [10]. This conflation has meaningful consequences for practice: educators may add gamified elements through implementation in the expectation that doing so will cause deep engagement like game-based learning, or conversely, they may deploy complex educational games when simpler gamification strategies can all that is needed to achieve their intended outcomes [11]. From a research perspective, the absence of comparative studies that also consider the differential effects these approaches have on specific motivational outcomes has led to fragmented evidence bases that provide only general guidance for instructional design [12]. Earlier studies have tended to focus on one approach in isolation, and many of them do not evaluate whether the motivational impact is due to the specific game elements or simply general pedagogical factors such as novelty (of games) or teacher enthusiasm [13]. Furthermore, most existing studies are limited to short-term engagement metrics that do not specify between intrinsic or extrinsic motivational pathways [14], creating an important gap in understanding how such approaches differentially shape students’ longer-term interest in STEM domains.Purpose and Research QuestionsThis research will help to fill this gap by systematically comparing the differential effects of gamification and game-based learning on student motivation in secondary STEM classrooms. Instead of viewing motivation as a unitary construct, this work separates intrinsic motivation (engagement due to inherent interest and pleasure) from extrinsic motivation (engagement driven by external incentives or performance pressures), reasoning that these different forms of motivation may respond differently to game-informed techniques [15]. Using a quasi-experimental design that delineates the aspects of the described intervention conditions, this study aims to provide empirical clarity on which approach produces better outcomes for some motivational targets. As such, this study is guided by the following research questions:RQ1: How does intrinsic motivation differ between the gamified group and the game-based learning group?RQ2: How do extrinsic motivation and task engagement in both conditions differ?RQ3: What do students feel about each approach in terms of enjoyment, relevance, and perceived learning? In particular, these questions aim to both quantify differences in motivational outcomes as well as qualitatively describe students’ subjective experiences, thereby providing a more holistic view of how each strategy plays out in real-life classroom scenarios.Significance of the StudyThis study contributes to the body of knowledge in educational technology, both theoretically and practically. What theoretically expands self-determination theory by exploring how different game-informed strategies satisfy or thwart learners’ basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness differentially [3]. Although self-determination theory has been applied widely to explain motivation in traditional and digital learning contexts, few studies have explicitly examined how the underlying structural differences between gamification and game-based learning can cater to these fundamental needs [16]. This study enhances our understanding of the mechanisms that may underlie these motivational processes by mapping intervention characteristics onto theoretical constructs. Practically, findings will yield actionable guidance for STEM educators, instructional designers, and curriculum developers who must choose appropriate approaches at the intersection of game design with informal learning [17]. For applications where instant task completion and behavioural engagement are important objectives, gamification serves as a low-resources solution; for situations where in-depth conceptualisation and an enduring interest in the subject are of greatest concern, game-based learning might reflect a higher payback [18]. Moreover, by deconstructing motivational results, this study provides practitioners with specific insights that could aid in aligning pedagogical practices with different learning aims and optimising both instructional efficiency and resource utilisation [19]. By doing so, this study furthers the larger mission of transforming STEM education from a source of student alienation to one defined by curiosity, persistence, and genuine intellectual delight [20].Literature ReviewTheoretical Framework: Self-Determination TheoryThe theoretical framework for this study is based on self-determination theory (SDT), a macro-theory of human motivation that has been widely adopted in educational contexts [21]. Self-Determination Theory (SDT) asserts that intrinsic motivation, doing an activity for its inherent satisfaction instead of some separable consequence, thrives when three basic psychological needs are fulfilled: autonomy, competence, and relatedness [3]. Autonomy is defined as the experience of volition and psychological freedom; competence relates to the sense of being effective in one’s interactions with the environment; and relatedness refers to experiencing a meaningful connection with others [22]. Just supporting these needs leads individuals to be more intrinsically motivated, engaged, and thrive; however, thwarting these needs shifts motivation towards controlled extrinsic forms or may even lead to a complete absence of motivation [23]. In educational contexts, SDT has also been especially useful for understanding how instructional practices succeed or fail in maintaining student interest [24]. Yet, traditional approaches to STEM teaching, rooted in one-size-fits-all curricula and extrinsic grading pressures, frequently undermine both autonomy and relatedness [25], thereby reinforcing the downward trajectory of student motivation that is observed across secondary education. In contrast, game-informed pedagogies may offer ways to fulfil these psychological needs through mechanisms like choice (autonomy), scaffolded challenge (competence), and collaborative or competitive structures (relatedness) [26]. Most critically, SDT makes a distinction between intrinsic motivation (engagement in an activity for its own sake) and extrinsic motivation (engagement through the prospect of separable consequences), which is vital to understanding the divergent effects of gamification and game-based learning [27]. This study utilises SDT as a theoretical framework to analyse how each approach exerts an effect on different motivational pathways.Gamification in Education: Definitions, Mechanisms, and Empirical FindingsGamification is essentially the application of game design elements within non-game contexts [6]. In education, it usually means adding motivational affordances like points, badges, leaderboards, progress bars, and challenges to existing curricular activities while keeping the instructional content intact [28]. Usual mechanisms by which gamification can affect motivation are mainly based on behavioural and extrinsic elements, such as receiving points for immediate feedback, awarding badges when achievements are accomplished, and competitive social benchmarking using leaderboards [8]. The relatively low cost of implementing gamification and the ease with which it can be included in traditional schooling frameworks fuelled early enthusiasm [4]. It has produced inconclusive empirical support for its effectiveness in motivating behaviour. Sailer and Homner also conducted a meta-analysis of gamification studies that yielded small to moderate positive effects on cognitive, motivational, and behavioural outcomes across the studies; however, they noted significant variance in effect size as a function of contextual factors and implementation quality [29]. The most consistent positive effects are seen in extrinsic motivation and task completion metrics, with points and badges having reliable effects on how long participants engage for and participation rates [30]. However, concerns have been raised regarding the sustainability of such effects: high rates of extrinsic reinforcement may actually disrupt intrinsic motivation, a phenomenon termed the overjustification effect [31]. Furthermore, leaderboards can have harmful effects on motivation for low achievers due to decreased competence [32]. Qualitative research indicates that students do not consider gamified components as meaningful and perceive them to be superficial or manipulative when there is no incorporation with learning objectives [33]. These findings indicate that although gamification may prove beneficial in terms of driving behavioural engagement, it is still unclear whether this intervention has the capacity to facilitate deeper intrinsic interest around STEM content.Game-Based Learning: Definitions, Characteristics, and Empirical FindingsGame-based learning (GBL) is the use of fully developed digital or analog games as the main means for delivering educational material and developing skills [5]. In contrast with gamification, which adds a layer of game elements on top of existing instruction, GBL incorporates learning objectives into the core game mechanics, narrative structure in games, and problem-solving challenges [34]. Some essential features of good educational games are meaningful storytelling to give context, authentic tasks that require using knowledge, progressively increasing difficulty to cause flow, and chances to explore or discover [35]. The theoretical underpinning of GBL is rooted in constructivism, from which the notion that learners create understanding via active participation in authentic, situated contexts [36] emerges. The empirical data have largely confirmed the effectiveness of GBL in improving motivation and learning outcomes. A comprehensive meta-analysis conducted by Clark and co-authors has shown that games consistently outperformed traditional instruction for both learning and retention across a variety of subjects, with particularly strong effect sizes for STEM subjects [37]. In relation to motivation, GBL has been linked with enhanced situational interest, perceived autonomy, and effort in difficult tasks [38]. In particular, the purported immersive quality of narrative-driven games likely satisfies a psychological need for relatedness through identification with characters and meaningful social interactions in-game [39]. Longitudinal research has shown that GBL results in long-lasting effects on motivation towards STEM careers when games include authentic practices of science, such as experimentation and modelling [40]. Implementation challenges have included increased development costs, extended time commitments, and the necessity for teacher training to implement game-based experiences effectively [41]. Furthermore, bad game designs (those that underemphasize pedagogy in favour of fun) can lead to engagement but no better learning gains [42]. The evidence indicates that GBL is more effective than gamification for cultivating intrinsic motivation and deep conceptual understanding despite these challenges.Comparative Studies: Review of Existing Research Contrasting the Two ApproachesAlthough there is now a significant amount of research on both gamification and GBL, little research directly compares their different effects on motivation within the same methodological frame [12]. The comparative literature is limited in both quantity and scope. In a study by de-Marcos and colleagues, the effectiveness of a gamified learning platform was tested against serious games in relation to information literacy instruction, finding that while the game produced better learning outcomes, a greater impression of perceived enjoyment was found with a gamified approach [43]. In contrast, a study by Su and Cheng found that elementary science learners exposed to game-based learning exhibited significantly greater learning motivation and self-efficacy than those who received gamified instruction [44]. These contradictory findings indicate that contextual factors such as age group, domain of study, and fidelity of implementation moderate the relative success of either approach. However, a recent systematic review by Li et al [12] identified only twelve empirical studies that directly compared gamification and game-based learning in any educational context, concluding that the evidence base is still too fragmentary to draw firm conclusions. The primary gaps in the research included: (a) a failure to differentiate between intrinsic and extrinsic motivational outcomes, (b) little use of studies including control groups with no-game treatment conditions to control for novelty effects, (c) few examining whether different subgroups of students (based on factors such as prior gaming experience or academic achievement) might benefit from approaches differently; and (d) qualitative data capturing students’ subjective experience with each approach was lacking [14]. Moreover, most comparative studies used pre-existing games or gamified platforms that vary on multiple other dimensions besides the central dichotomy of approach used, adding confounding variables that limit interpretability [45]. This research fills these gaps by creating interventions that hold content, length, and instructor attributes constant while systematically varying the game-informed strategy.Hypotheses DevelopmentFrom the theoretical framework and empirical literature discussed, we propose the following hypotheses. Firstly, regarding intrinsic motivation, GBL is theorised to fulfil the psychological needs for competence and relatedness due to its immersive and autonomy-supportive characteristics more effectively than gamification’s predominantly extrinsic mechanisms [5], [38].
